en: The Commentary on the *Śrī-Buddhakapāla-Mahātantrarāja*, titled *Abhayapaddhati*:
The First Chapter, on the Bursting Open of the Skull that Emanates the Book Determining All Accomplishments and Knowledge; Homage to Śrī-Vajrasattva!

The enemy of existence (*bhavāri*), whose form is supreme bliss, enriched by the unfolding of the diverse armies of the Goddess, and who sports with the splendor of the immeasurable Mother of the World as she flashes forth with unrestrained radiance at the end of the aeon.

Thus Abhaya makes it clear that this path is to be cultivated by those of virtuous conduct through a mental state radiant with the essence of innate bliss, the splendor of perfect enlightenment. || 1 ||
At the command of the Vajra goddesses heard in a dream, I, rendered fearless through their empowerment, compose this commentary on this *Buddhakapāla*. (2)
Surely I have been empowered today by that Lord, the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, since his words seem to speak for my own benefit as they reach my ears. (3)

O virtuous ones, embrace joy; O holy men, cast away the grief of those who rise up [in passion]. O darkness that dwells within the three worlds, depart far away from you who look only toward the mundane!
A certain light, the abode of Dharma and the path to fearlessness, arises for one who reflects with equanimity and touches upon incomparable prosperity.

Of this *Buddhakapālatantra*, which consists of fourteen chapters, the Blessed Lord Buddhakapāla is both the teacher (*deśaka*) and the subject matter (*abhidheya*). Thus, the relationship between the teacher and the taught, as well as the relationship between the expression (*abhidhāna*) and the expressed (*abhidheya*), have been stated. Furthermore, the purpose (*prayojana*) for those to be trained is the realization of the meaning of the *Buddhakapāla*.
This [purpose] is characterized by the single flavor of vajra-like great bliss (*mahāsukha*) that benefits the entire world; it is understood from the colophons (*puṣpikā*).
And the names of the chapters have been taken from the Tibetan translation of the root text of the *Śrī Buddhakapāla Tantra*.
The purpose of the purpose [of this work] is the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā, titled *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the great king of tantras, the *Śrī Buddhakapāla*.
In that regard, the introduction begins with "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā*) and ends with "they were" (*abhūvan*).
For when this [condition] exists, there is the occurrence of the teaching;
for the assembly of time, place, teacher, and audience is the primary cause of the teaching,
since without these, the teaching is impossible.
In that regard, the Blessed One stated in the *Dharmasaṅgīti-sūtra*: "Thus have I [heard]—in this manner my Dharma is to be compiled; it should be undertaken according to such a sequence.
Therefore, the compiler recited it in exactly that way.
Who is the compiler here? What is the purpose of this inquiry into his identity?

By virtue of being spoken by him at the command of the Blessed One, these words are indeed the speech of the Blessed One himself; furthermore, because the tantra has been entrusted to him here, he is called Vajrapāṇi.
In this context, the particle *evam* (thus) illuminates the entire meaning of the tantra that is about to be recited as being unerring.
Therefore, this very word *evam* encompasses the entire meaning of the tantra.

And they teach that because the meaning of the tantra consists of wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*), it abides as the essential nature of the two syllables. "By me" (*mayā*) means the recitation was performed by me.
"Hear" (*śrutam*) means understood through the auditory consciousness according to the phonemes and through the mental consciousness according to the meaning.
"This was not realized by me directly; rather, it is because the Blessed One has attained this Dharma in all its aspects"—thus he demonstrates his reverence for the Dharma.
Having thus introduced the subject in general terms, he now shows it specifically and in sequence, beginning with "At one time," and so forth.

"One" refers to a certain [Buddha] who possesses the equipment of merit and knowledge that cannot be accomplished by others; it is an inconceivable particularity of time that cannot be delimited by lunar days, constellations, and the like.
Furthermore, in this context, that which consists of the fourth moment is designated as "time" (*samaya*).
By modifying the phrasing of the expression "at that one time the Blessed One was staying," the connection is made as "he was staying.
He is called the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) because he possesses fortune (*bhaga*).
Furthermore, those qualities are sovereignty and the rest.
As it has been said:
"Of complete sovereignty, beauty, fame, and fortune..."
The Śruti states that "bhaga" refers to knowledge, purpose, and effort—these six qualities.
Alternatively, he is the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) because he has conquered the four Māras.

Or else, *bhaga* is the wisdom that increases all dharmas and destroys the Māra of the afflictions and so forth; since he possesses this [wisdom] here through identity (*tādātmyena*), he is the Blessed One.
As it is said in the *Vajraśekhara-tantra*: "Those afflictions are to be slain by wisdom; therefore, wisdom is called Bhagavatī.

[End of First Chapter] "All those Tathāgatas" refers to Akṣobhya and the others; their body, speech, and mind are the Vajra, which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). That form is the "Great Ornament" (*mahālaṃkāra*), because it possesses the great capacity (*alam*) for the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others, and its function (*kriyā*) or activity (*vyāpāra*) is unsurpassed.

Vajragarbha is the essence of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*). That which takes or grasps its *maṇḍa*—the core, which is the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*)—is the *maṇḍala*, namely the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*).

The bodies, speech, and minds of all Tathāgatas, as well as that *vajramahālaṃkāramaṇḍala*, possess the nature of the body, speech, and mind of all Tathāgatas because they are of one taste (*ekarasa*).
For this very reason, it is triangular; in its center...
Although the gabled pavilion (kūṭāgāra) is not explicitly mentioned here, it should be understood by the sense that it is situated in the center of the source of phenomena (dharmodayā).
For example, the phrase "the residence of a wealthy man in a city" implies the palace located within that city.
It is not stated in that way [here] for the purpose of demonstrating the preeminence of the stage of great bliss (mahāsukhabhūmi).
For even that gabled chamber (*kūṭāgāra*) is of a single flavor.
Alternatively, "vajra" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*); within that is the great adorned maṇḍala-gabled chamber.

In the midst of that, by demonstrating the Blessed One's abiding in such a place, the innate body (*sahajakāya*), which is the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion, is to be understood with clarity.
And by that very body, the teaching of the tantra is also shown to be of one single flavor.
Thus, the perfection of the time, place, and teacher has been stated; now he speaks of the perfection of the assembly, beginning with the words "all," and so forth.
It was blessed by the Tathāgatas such as Akṣobhya, by yoginīs such as Citrasenā, and by [disciples] such as Āryānanda.

The mention of those free from passion (vītarāga) is for the purpose of indicating that this applies to the Śrāvakayāna followers as well; it is to make known that even for those of the Pāramitāyāna, the Vajrayāna alone is the attainment of enlightenment consisting of great bliss (mahāsukha).
Furthermore, Lokeśvara and others were present there.

And this introductory statement has been explained by us in detail, as appropriate, in the *Śrīsampuṭa-ṭīkā*; let the wise take note. Then, with the words beginning "At that time" (*atha*), the compiler introduces the Blessed One’s teaching in accordance with that introduction.

Vajradhara is he who holds the five gnoses, which are the nature of emptiness; thus, he is the non-dual unity of emptiness and compassion, whose intrinsic nature is innate great bliss (*sahaja-mahāsukha*).

Mahāmudrā, whose single flavor is great bliss and which benefits the world, is emptiness itself; it is the "vajra" because it pierces all obscurations. It is also the "state" (pada), being the foundation for the perfection of the welfare of oneself and others.
That very [teaching] has been excellently taught by all the tantras and mantras as being supremely worthy of adoption because it is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
By this, he is indicated to be the "Lord" (*svāmī*)—the master (*svāmin*) of all the Tathāgatas, such as Vairocana and the others.
Through his status as Lord, he indicates that he is the unsurpassed Teacher (*śāstṛ*).
The vajra is one's own self, and the lotus belongs to Citrasenā; through the union of these two,
the woman is Citrasenā,
and her bhaga is the source of phenomena (dharmodayā).
Internally, however, the *vajra* is the *bodhicitta*, and the *padma*, *uṣṇīṣa*, and so forth are the *bhagas* of the woman, that is, of the *avadhūtī*.
"Parinirvṛta" means having become fluid in the form of *bodhicitta*.
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), however, the woman is *prajñā*.
Citrasenā is Samantabhadrā under another name;
her *bhaga* is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The plural number is used because Citrasenā embodies the gathering of all women.

There, by means of the Mahāmudrā-vajrapada, the Blessed One did not remain in existence through wisdom; rather, out of compassion, he did not abide in cessation, but was thus completely extinguished through non-abiding nirvāṇa. This is the commentary on the *Śrībuddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja* titled *Abhayapaddhati*.

Having become identical with that through the nature of a single fusion, because of the non-recognition of all distinctions, and being free from conceptual construction, one remains—by virtue of prior momentum—in the state of "What shall I do for all sentient beings? together with the infinite Tathāgatas, Bodhisattvas, Yoginīs, Vītarāgas, Mudrās, Maṇḍalas, and Mantras numbering eighty million, throughout the duration of saṃsāra; this is the meaning.

Nevertheless, this Dharma which I have realized is supremely profound; moreover, sentient beings for the most part possess little merit and poor wisdom, and are inclined toward the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Therefore, thinking, "Who will even believe in this? he was indifferent and lacked the enthusiasm to teach the Dharma he had realized, being occupied with his own welfare and lacking diligence—this is what is meant by being inactive and lacking zeal regarding the state of neither remaining in cyclic existence nor in peace. The phrase "that" refers to both that state of not remaining in either existence or peace and that lack of enthusiasm. Having attained a state of wonder, he thought: "I am endowed with supreme compassion and wisdom; established as I am in the right principle, how can I be without enthusiasm? Thus he was struck with amazement.

"Citrasenā" means she whose *senā*—that is, her great bliss (*mahāsukha*)—is "citra," meaning variegated, diverse, and wonderful; she is thus the Yoginī. Yoga is defined as the meditative union (*samāpatti*) of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*).
Being exceedingly fortunate, she asks because she is capable of answering questions:
"Is there some means by which sentient beings may obtain power—the capacity to accomplish the welfare of themselves and others?
The purpose [of this teaching] is the instruction on mantras and methods in the Tantras and other scriptures."
He states this doubt with the words beginning "muṣṭi" (the fist), etc.
Herein is the summary of the meaning.
Regarding those tantras and other scriptures taught by the Lord of Sages, efficacy is not observed therein without mantra; yet, many doubts arise concerning mantra.
For instance, there is the recitation of mantra through ten million, one hundred thousand, or ten thousand repetitions, respectively, for beings of inferior, middling, and superior merit.
This is according to the reading: "beings who are possessed by passion."
The word "of them" (*teṣām*) is to be supplied [as the subject].
For those who are ignorant, even though the recitation of tantras and mantras might involve counting by means of written marks, how could it be done with a defiled mind?

Even for one possessing right knowledge (*samyagjñānin*), the mind is fixed upon and examined as having completely transcended the extremes of existence and non-existence; in this sense, the suffix *-niṣṭha* is placed at the end of the compound.

What is his mantra? Therefore, the mantra is that which is to be recited by the practitioner; thus, it is the mantra to be recited through the ritual action of mantra. Consequently, the mind is focused upon it. "Man" is the act of thinking, and "tra" is protection; thus, the ultimate mantra is the gnosis inseparable from emptiness and compassion, because from that alone the capacity for the welfare of oneself and others is accomplished. The sense is: what is the use of the mere recitation of mantra?
Regarding the question "how" in all cases:
a discerning person should not recite [the mantra] in the manner thus described.
Even there, if there is recitation, success is attained; otherwise, there is no success.
"Tārākalpakoṭi" uses the nominative case in the sense of the instrumental;
that is, for an immeasurable number of ten-million eons (kalpakoṭi), like the immeasurable stars in the sky.
"Tathā" means "just as."
First Chapter: When doubt exists, recitation (japa) is not possible; likewise, even if recitation occurs, success (siddhi) may sometimes fail due to uncertainty regarding the meaning and so forth.
Regarding the term "Bhagavantī":
she is the Great Goddess (Mahādevī), the foremost queen of the Bhagavān; therefore, like the Bhagavān himself, she is the sovereign of all tantras by virtue of her fitness to teach all tantras.
For it has been stated that this [goddess], in the form of Vajravārāhī, is the instructor of the *Lakṣābhidhāna* and the *Vajraḍāka-tantras*;
the meaning is that the Blessed One is [referred to] by her,
because she is the Sovereign (*īśvarī*) due to her possession of an unimpeded and inconceivable power in all respects.
"She was thus [rescued] by the Blessed One merely by being looked upon"— that is, by the Blessed One's mere looking.

Regarding "kapāla": because it protects (*pālayati*) bliss (*kaṃ*) from the skull (*kapāla*), it is called *kapāla*; this refers to the seed-syllable of the bodhicitta, the unstruck sound (*anāhata*). From that, the mantra issues forth.

Because of the statement, "In this regard, one should meditate upon that seed of gnosis in the form of a *bindu* between the eyebrows," one should stabilize the mind in the form of a *bindu* at the midpoint of the eyebrows through meditation, and from there emanate the mantra;
or else, [emanate] those belonging to the Blessed One.
From the *kapāla* [of] Citrasenā, which is the *dharmodayā*; as he will say: "Her *kapāla*-maṇḍala is well-established through mantra and tantra"—this is the traditional teaching (*āmnāya*) here:

from the *anāhata* [center] situated in the Blessed One’s wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), having issued forth by the downward path of the *avadhūtī*, it enters the Blessed Lady’s *dharmodayā*. Then, from the middle of the brows at the lower end of the *avadhūtī*, there is the emergence of the mantra in the forward order (*anuloma*) and its entry in the reverse order (*pratiloma*).
This very meaning has been clarified by the passage beginning with "in this way" and ending with "entered into the skull. Regarding the term *vidhvaṃsate* (is destroyed/dissolved):

having shaken [the winds] (*vidhūya*), "Citrasenā" refers to the *avadhūtī* channel of the Blessed Lady Citrasenā. Having entered its opening at the center of the eyebrows, [the seminal essence] melts together with the *bodhicitta* and enters downward into the interior of the skull, which is the *dharmodayā*.
Having emerged from there, [the wind] enters through the *anāhata* [cakra] by way of the Lord’s vajra-path in reverse order.
"This is the [wind] of these *nāgas*"—this is the connection; all *nāgas* are "greatly powerful" (*mahārddhika*).
This refers to Vāsuki, Karkoṭaka, and others, whoever they may be, from whom arise those poisons produced from venom that exist as poison emitted through sight, fangs, saliva, touch, or fire.
"O Queen, we have been commanded; as we were speaking,
Citrasenā said:"
Thus, immediately upon hearing "Buddha" and so forth,

the skull of the Blessed One, having been explained, bursts open and expands; from the bindu situated between the eyebrows— which is by nature the *āli* and *kāli*— a book, whose nature is the compendium of all phenomena (*sarvadharmasamuccaya*) and which consists of leaves with a collection of scripts, emerges like a mantra.
Alternatively, "pu" refers to Pullīramalaya; "sta" means that which brings nourishment (*puṣṭikara*); and "ka" means happiness (*sukha*). Thus, "pustaka" refers to the *bodhicitta*.
The meaning is that this very *bodhicitta* becomes a book consisting of written leaves.

Because of the explanation of the repetition as "in space," when there is the sound— the resonance (*nāda*)— at the time of the union of the vajra and lotus in space, which is the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*), then the book emerges;
that very thing is the sound being produced by the gods in space.
"Tantra" means a continuous composition (*prabandha*); furthermore, it is threefold due to the distinction between cause, fruit, and means.
Among these, the state of being Heruka, which is without beginning or end, is the *hetu-tantra* (cause-tantra).

Taking that very [cause] as the basis, there is the commentary on the *Śrī Buddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja* titled *Abhayapaddhati*. Because Phalaheruka arises from it, and because adventitious defilements are removed, he acts for the benefit of the entire world; thus, Phalaheruka is the *phalatantra*.
The means for the purification of that very [result] is the *upāyatantra*.
Methods such as the *gāruḍa-yoga* are means only insofar as they are auxiliary to the primary means;

the direct means, however, is the practice as described through the application of the *mudrā* at the time of attaining the accomplishment of *mahāmudrā*. For that [practice], the *utpannakrama* (completion stage) is the direct means, and for that, the *utpattikrama* (generation stage).
"Great King" (*mahārāja*) refers to his delighting of sentient beings by accomplishing the great perfection of the welfare of both self and others;
"benefiting all sentient beings" is its detailed explanation,
and "bringing happiness to all sentient beings" is its further specification.

Regarding the term *sarvasiddhi*: since all accomplishments (*siddhis*) proceed from this, it is the *Yoginīyāna*; it is the *Yoginītantra* because they go (*yānti*) to it, and also because they go by means of it (*yānti anena*). Thus, he indicates that its nature consists of the fruit, the cause, and the means, and that it is unsurpassed (*niruttara*).
Regarding the phrase "bestowing swift results," he first indicates the generation stage (*utpannakrama*) as the direct means therein,
beginning with the word *stobha*. *Stobha*...
The raised vajra,
however, is the bodhicitta within;
the lotus is the pillar because it serves as its support.
That which is born from that is the co-emergent great gnosis (*mahājñāna*) by virtue of being the aggregate of all phenomena;
it is the unsurpassed state (*niruttara-pada*) by virtue of being unobscured great bliss. "State" (*pada*) means a station, because of the perfection of the welfare of oneself and others.
The state devoid of the movement of the channels is difficult to attain for those afflicted by laziness and other such faults;
it is a secret not to be revealed to the Śrāvakas and others.
Therefore, because it is the domain only of those with supremely exalted and sharp wisdom who have accumulated merit,
it is delightful, endowed with bliss and other qualities, and established throughout the entire body.
He states that because of the uninterrupted experience of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) everywhere, there is a complete clarity [of it],
since the body itself arises as having that single flavor, just as a wave [arises] from water.
Thus, by virtue of pervading all things, the Lord of the Mandala (*maṇḍaleśa*) is taught as being accompanied by the deities of the mandala (*māṇḍaleya*).
He indicates the branch of skillful means beginning with "Gāruḍa" and so forth; from "killing" onwards, he indicates the twelve activities and the generation stage.
"Various mantras" refers to the seed-syllables for generation and so forth, such as *hūṃ*,
according to the rule stated in the chapter to be explained hereafter,
for the yoginīs beginning with Citrasenā.
According to their arising and according to their application, there is the origination of Heruka;
and the cause of the origination of Heruka, the Great Hero, is the moon and so forth.
The cause of stability is the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*) and so forth;
this is the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), which is to be meditated upon first.
For here, in the Mantra Mahāyāna, it is precisely the meditation on the form of the deity that is taught for the initial entry of beginner practitioners.
As it is said: "The meditation on the form of the deity is taught in the first tantra for the sake of accomplishing all activities for beginner beings"—this is the first chapter.

To demonstrate that the completion stage (*utpannakrama*) is the direct goal of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), and what kind of generation stage serves as the means, he next states the distinction between the two stages by way of an outline of the generation stage.

Regarding the passage beginning with "bhāva" and so forth: because there is an absence of both existence and non-existence—which are superimposed and which pervade all other superimpositions—there is the "absence of the proliferation of existence and non-existence.

Since there is no determination based on the presence or absence of the two obscurations, one might ask: "In that case, is there not the performance of the welfare of others, as in the nirvāṇa of the Śrāvakas? To this, he says: "the prison of existence."

Even though they are free from obscurations, out of great compassion for the sake of others, they take up cyclic existence for an infinite duration; as it is said in the *Paramādya-tantra*: "As long as the noble heroes remain dwelling within cyclic existence, so long are they capable of performing incomparable benefit for sentient beings, remaining without [personal] nirvāṇa."
Thus,
he again indicates the limb of skillful means with the words "the intentional language" (saṃdhyābhāṣa), and so forth.

The twelve rites beginning with *pratimasya* and ending with *khaḍga* are taught by means of the description of preceding and subsequent rites; this indicates that for one established in the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) and one established in the completion stage (*utpannakrama*), all rites are accomplished through the *Buddhakapāla* yoga.
For this very reason, the two [rites] of killing and subduing are included as representative examples.
Regarding "disappearance" (*antardhyāna*), it refers to oneself as being inferior or lowly.
"By difficult and severe observances, the body withers and becomes afflicted;
from affliction the mind is distracted, and from distraction, accomplishment is otherwise.
Thus he said.
When the five objects of desire are enjoyed,
among all illusions, the illusion of women is preeminent;
this very distinction of the three types of knowledge is clearly perceived right here.

According to this principle, while the five objects of desire are being enjoyed, the primary [object] is the service of women; through skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), she is the cause for the attainment of Mahāmudrā.
Therefore, he speaks in order to explain the aphrodisiac (*vājīkaraṇa*) for that purpose:

"Ghoramadi" refers to a great battle capable of crushing the terrible conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) at the moment they arise spontaneously; it is a variety of sexual delight performed by a single man in which he conquers a hundred thousand women. To the question, "Is such a thing seen in reality through the use of aphrodisiacs (*vājīkaraṇa*)?", he says:
Regarding the title *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the great king of tantras, the *Śrībuddhakapāla*:

"by a single man" means that one man, being a great lover (*mahākāmī*), is seen to overcome a hundred thousand women—this being the implication, as the sixty-eight thousand women beginning with the noble Dharmodgatā are used as an illustration;
therefore, he should desire [them].
"By one" means one;
"all" means all.
And here, the method is *vājīkaraṇa* (aphrodisiac therapy), which consists of the melting, retention, and increase of the *bodhicitta*.
We shall explain how these three come to be by means of the passage beginning with "ataḥ," wherein he points out the *Gāruḍa* [Tantra] according to its name.
I shall explain it as it is well known:
the preparation of *śāliki* and the preparation of *vidyādhara* are now being specifically described;
[it concerns] gambling with dice, and thereafter, play which neutralizes poison.
Beating a drum,
the abduction of a woman by one who has been bitten,
and striking with a *karavīra* wooden staff from the head down to the feet.
"Pāśa" means drawing [the bird] by tying it with a rope in the shape of a noose around its neck; "kokila-śabdoccāraṇa" means uttering the sound of a cuckoo;
and "padmosthāla" refers to the lotus-stand.
Within the internal lotuses, according to the instruction, there is the cessation of the wind by uprooting its support;

furthermore, he describes the constriction of the two channels of the *saṃbhoga-cakra* as "the tiger-making," which is an act of treading upon [the channels] through a simulated movement of treading like a tigress.
He points to the water as "the conch," which is the sound of the conch;
[he points to] the taking of the chalk as "the taking of the chalk."
By writing his name with chalk, there is the removal of poison and deliverance; by covering it with a cloth, there is vomiting.
"Carpaṭa" means striking with the palm;
"tryakṣara" means striking with the *ṭakkara* mantra;
and "ha ho hī"—by these three syllables, there is the destruction of poison, according to some.
Regarding the "discourse on the vision of meditative absorption," the discourse should be conducted through the vision of the cultivation of the white form and so forth;
by means of these eighteen applications, the extraction of poison occurs.
Thus he indicates what has been taught concerning the stage of completion (*utpannakrama*).
"From this," and so forth:
"divine" means that which arises in the lotus in the heaven of Sukhāvatī;
"knowledge" is innate bliss (*sahajānanda*). Just as [it is] devoid of a nature of being one or many, and thus lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), so too is conventional truth.

The *bhaga* is the lotus; situated within its center as the support, it remains having shaken off all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), because it does not abide in either cyclic existence or nirvana.
As it is said in the *Vajra*: "I dwell in Sukhāvatī, in the *bhaga* of the excellent Vajra-woman, which has the form of the letter *E*, the jewel-casket of the Buddhas."
Thus,
likewise,
regarding the Garuḍa-yoga: "O, he who is established by the name of *śukra* (semen) in the Sukhāvatī of the woman's womb."
"Without that, there would be no happiness; having abandoned happiness, one would exist through becoming.
Thus, "I am of the nature of innate bliss (sahajānanda), [consisting of] the supreme, the end, and the cessation, etc.
Here, by the name "semen" (śukra), it is because the mind itself, in the form of the thought of enlightenment (bodhicitta), is manifested in such a way.

"Paramānta-viramādikam" means that "virama" is the end of the supreme (*parama*) and is the beginning of what follows; thus, it refers to the bliss of cessation (*viramānanda*) immediately following the supreme, and after that, the innate (*sahaja*).
According to another school of thought, however, it refers to the beginning of cessation (*virama*).

The meaning is "in the interval between the supreme and the cessation. However, this view is inconsistent, because of the statement: "One should perceive [the bliss] at the beginning of cessation, devoid of the three other joys."

For by this it is established that since this [state] is both a cessation (*virama*) and the beginning (*ādi*), one should recognize the innate (*sahaja*), which is about to arise, at the very moment of cessation from the outset.
However, when the innate has arisen, because all conceptual constructions have set,
how could there be any defining characteristic?

For this very reason, by the venerable Ārya [Nāgārjuna] stating, "This differentiation of the three knowledges is clearly perceived right here," he has described both the definition and the non-definition of the fourth bliss through the description of the three blisses.

And by the Blessed One [it was stated]: "That which is devoid of characteristics is other than the three. Therefore, how can the *virama* arise immediately after the *sahaja*, given that it is characterized by incapacity?
If the definition were merely the recollection of the interval between cessations (*viramāntara*), then it would have been taught as a means for experiencing [the innate].

However, there is no disagreement regarding the locus of the arising of the innate (*sahaja*). But surely, even at the beginning, why is it not a definition? Precisely because it has not been experienced.
It is not like the twilight of the dawn.
[Objection: Even so, it is true that its form remains unperceived; nevertheless, this means of experience is taught in such a manner.
[Reply: But even as a means, it ought not to be thus.
From that time forward, because that [perception] is impossible for him due to his attachment to that indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*), it is true;
if it were thus, then the teachers will explain how one should act when it arises in that manner. In this way, the sequence of indicative marks has been indicated in both views.

If the *virama* were immediately followed by the *sahaja*, then the other tantras—[which speak of] the holder of sixteen, eight, and four drops (*bindu*), as well as the accomplishment of the *mudrā*—would be contradicted;
furthermore, the means for experiencing the *sahaja* would not be possible.

Those who know the tradition state that it is the very nature of the *sahaja* alone that is not contradicted; this is the previously established view. Enough of this digression, concludes the *Abhayapaddhati*, the commentary on the *Śrī Buddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja*.
That divine gnosis, being an example, should be understood as the mundane, innate means for achieving the goal of great bliss (*mahāsukha*); thus it is said to be "the bestower of great bliss.
When that innate state, which serves as the means, is practiced according to the instructions, it produces the goal—the immutable, unobscured, and unsurpassed great bliss.

Regarding these two types of gnosis—the bliss of the means and the bliss of the goal—their reality (*tattva*) is nothing other than emptiness (*śūnyatā*), characterized by the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvābhāvya*).

However, for those who remain convinced that pleasure itself is the ultimate reality, the Blessed One spoke in order to dispel their delusion: "Therefore, pleasure is not called the ultimate reality, because pleasure is a great element (*mahābhūta*);
even that which is innate does not exist at all times or in all places."

For instance, the innate nature of things is ultimately emptiness itself; the conventional is consciousness. As for bliss, even if it were indeed consciousness, it would still not be innate at all times or in all places, because it is not experienced during the experience of suffering or equanimity, nor in the fourth dhyāna or the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu), just as consciousness is not experienced there.
As it is said in the *Nāmasaṅgīti*: "The one who holds the pinnacle of the fourth dhyāna."

In this context, the meaning is that because he abides in identity with the limit of the fourth dhyāna—the pinnacle of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) which is free from all stains of conceptual construction—he "bears its very nature.

When the three realms, consisting of infinite [beings], manifest as composed of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), then even the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*) and so forth consist of great bliss; this belongs to the Blessed One alone and not to anyone else. Thus it is said, and the repetition is for the sake of clarification.

How, then, is bliss said to be innate? Just as great compassion, though without an objective referent, is cultivated by one who has not yet seen reality through the resolve that it exists; for one who has realized reality, its conventional nature is called innate because it consists of awakening.

Likewise, bliss— whether in the state of experiencing it or the state of not experiencing it— is called "worldly," "conventional," and "innate" (*sāṃvṛta-sahaja*) during the stage of attaining the realization of reality by one who has not yet seen the truth, through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*), while meditating on that reality whose nature is inseparable from great compassion, which consists of emptiness and is endowed with the excellence of all aspects.
However, when experienced during the stage of non-attainment of reality, it is worldly, conventional, and innate, because it merely follows the shadow of the innate.
And so it has been said: "That which is produced from the two innate [parents] is called 'innate' (sahaja);
innate is said to be the intrinsic nature (svabhāva), the single vow of all aspects."
The yogin who is free from causes through the mudrā is compassion; that which is inseparable from emptiness and compassion is known as bodhicitta. Thus it is said.
It is called *saṃvara* because things are gathered (*saṃkriyante*) within it.
It is the single, non-dual *saṃvara* of all aspects, such as blue, yellow, and so forth,
because the innate (*sahaja*) itself appears in those various ways.
Furthermore, that which is produced by the two innate [factors] is called "innate. Those two are the seal of compassion (*kṛpāmudrā*).
Therefore, one should become such a yogi whose means (*upāya*) is that great compassion consisting of great bliss, which has compassion as its objective support.
This has been stated:
this bliss is the reality of the means (upāya), but not the reality of wisdom (prajñā).
The seal (mudrā) is emptiness; it is the supreme wisdom characterized by the non-arising of all phenomena, because of the absence of a cause due to the separation from a cause.
Because all phenomena are unarisen from the very beginning,
these two natures are indeed innate, as they are established by themselves.
The reality arising from these two is the bodhicitta, which is the indivisibility of emptiness and compassion.
Is this, then, something other than the knowledge of wisdom (*prajñājñāna*)?
It is not other; rather, it is the very nature of that [knowledge] itself, revealed by the removal of its opposing factors, such that it is described as being "of such a kind."
This very bodhicitta, which arises from the practice of the two innate [wisdoms] whose nature is insight-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), is the fourth, the Mahāmudrā initiation;
for by means of this, all stains of conceptual construction are directly washed away.
As it has been said: "The fourth is likewise that."
Showing that the very nature of the universe is innate (*sahaja*), he says "tatraiva" and so forth.
"In that very [state]" means abiding through identity within that divine gnosis, which has as its sole flavor the emptiness that is free from all superimpositions such as existence and non-existence.
"All" refers to the "fools," namely ordinary worldly beings (*pṛthagjana*).

But how is it that they do not even know the nature of the Self? For they are deluded; "delusion" (moha) is the arising of ignorance, which consists of the erroneous grasping at existence, non-existence, and so forth. That very [Self] is knowledge, the essence, and great bliss, because it is the elixir (*rasāyana*) that causes the nourishment of qualities such as strength and fearlessness.
The meaning is that it is superior to external flavors and so forth due to its particular excellence (*turviśeṣe*).

Being practiced in that very way, it bestows great bliss; just as the Buddhas—through the awakening to the reality of the object which possesses diverse forms and is devoid of existence and non-existence—are established as consisting of the knowledge of the powers, fearlessnesses, and so forth, by virtue of their stainless purity.
In the *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the *Śrībuddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja*, the Dharma-kāya, whose nature is the Mind-vajra, is thus described.

The *maṇḍala* is that which has various forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth; it is the inseparable union of emptiness and compassion (*śūnyatā-karuṇā*), the form of the deity entered into meditative equipoise, distinguished by the divisions of joy (*ānanda*) and so on. It performs the emanation and withdrawal of the nature of birth and death, arising and cessation; it is the form of Vajrasattva, the *maṇḍala-cakra*, consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the divine, arisen form. He says, "In that very place, the sprinkling of the excellent disciple," because the fourth meaning itself, when being cultivated, becomes the perfected fourth consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
As for the sprinkling in the center of the *bhaga* according to the generation stage (*utpatti-krama*), he will explain that later.
Regarding *Heruka*: the Blessed One Heruka is the nature of the *saṃbhogakāya*.

In the Pāramitā system, the *saṃbhogakāya* is precisely that body which consists of the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, serving as the limb of the enjoyment of the Dharma through the teaching of the profound and vast Dharma to the Bodhisattvas who are lords of the ten stages. Here, however, by virtue of the *dharmakāya*, he is called the *nirmāṇakāya* when he is manifested in various forms such as Heruka and so forth, in accordance with those to be trained (*vineya*).
As for that which is called the "emanated Buddha" or *nirmāṇakāya* in the Pāramitā system, [it is here subsumed within this category].

Thus, here too, it is just like that, as if emanated (*nirmita*). Although the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is an emanation of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), in the Pāramitā system its distinctness arises precisely from the enjoyment of the Dharma. Here, however, it has the nature of speech; nevertheless, it possesses the quality of being an enjoyment body because of the enjoyment of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Furthermore, he is a "hero" (*vīra*) because all opposing factors have been uprooted. And within the inner mandala, he is the "lord" (*adhipati*) because he protects the Dharma through the speech of Dharma by drinking the flavor of great bliss (*mahāsukha-rasa*) along with the twenty-four goddesses who are about to be described.

He is the Lord (*prabhu*) because of his power to accomplish the welfare of others through the manifestation of various bodies without limit. The supreme means for neutralizing poison is the *Garuḍa* [mantra], which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*) itself.
As he will say: "When all phenomena are empty, how can there be snake venom?"

The word "tataḥ" (from that) refers to the fact that for those who lack conviction in emptiness (*śūnyatā*), it is a cause of fear; thus, it is the "terrible sādhana of the Daityas. Indeed, there is nothing in which the practitioner of the yoga of knowledge does not become master. Regarding the term "cremation ground" (*śmaśāna*): in the context of the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), it is the "abode of corpses" according to etymological rules. It is the dwelling place of corpses that illuminates the *dharmadhātu*, characterized by selflessness (*nairātmya*); we shall describe this as being delimited by the number eight. However, here, the body itself, which is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*, is the eight-limbed cremation ground.

In the Pāramitā-naya, it is stated that the appearance of Buddhas occurs over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*); however, here [in the Mantra-naya], he says it is at an indefinite time, stating: "The cause for instantaneous arising" and "those possessing great supernatural power (*mahārddhika*) within the three-thousandfold world systems.

Those who possess great supernatural power—meaning great miraculous powers (*mahā-ṛddhi*) consisting of immeasurable and diverse emanated forms—within the world systems of the three-thousandfold and so forth, are described as such.
By this, the body of emanation is called the Body-Vajra (*kāyavajra*).
He states that its very nature exists even in the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) with the words "world-systems" (*lokadhātu*); [that is,] the world-systems.
"That very one" refers to Mahāmudrā.
She is the Goddess because she is the locus of supreme bliss;
she is the mother of all Buddhas, having the nature of the causal state.

The great fortune (*mahālakṣmī*) of the bodhisattvas has the nature of the accumulations of merit and wisdom; in the state of fruition, it is the first chapter. Regarding "devoted to the perfection of wisdom" (*prajñāpāraparāyaṇī*): *parāyaṇī* means having gone completely to the limit of excellence in the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāre prakarṣaparyante*), which is the meaning of "perfection of wisdom" (*prajñāpāramitā*).
Regarding "the gate of hell":
for those who reject that [teaching], as it is said in the *Rājaratnāvalī*:—

Furthermore, another fool, due to his failure to understand this [teaching], imagining himself a scholar, has his soul destroyed by his own rejection [of it] and goes headfirst down to the Avīci hell.
Thus, that very [realization]— the removal of all obscurations— is liberation.

The fourth body is Mahāmudrā, which consists of great bliss whose nature is non-referential great compassion having the single flavor of emptiness; it accomplishes the welfare of the entire world without exception,
possesses great renown because the other three bodies are composed of this very essence,
and is therefore desirous of the benefit of all sentient beings.
Because her nature is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*),

she is the "mother" (*jananī*) since she gives birth to the universe in the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*); because she has arisen through the cultivation of the distinction between the conventional and ultimate truths (*saṃvṛti-paramārtha-satya*), she is the "sister's daughter" (*bhāgineyī*).
She is the "Sister" because she explains the distinction between the conventional and ultimate truths;
she is the "Daughter" because she milks and produces the unsurpassed qualities such as the powers (*bala*) and fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), which are like a cow of plenty (*dhenū*) in the sky;
and she is a "Woman" because she inspires attachment through unsurpassed bliss. Thus, she is *strī*.

Because she reveals the latent tendencies through the perfection of wisdom and, by acting accordingly, causes all sentient beings to be filled with affection, wisdom itself is called the "woman," and she is called the "one who moves among men" because she is exceedingly fickle toward men; for she offers herself to every sentient being for the sake of supreme, boundless, and limitless great bliss that flows from her unsurpassed compassion.
Alternatively, because it is impossible to stabilize the minds of beginner beings,
the realization of non-conceptual wisdom (*prajñā-niṣprapañca*) is what is meant by the "Great Seal" (*mahāmudrā*) of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).
These are the unsurpassed mudrās; furthermore, thirteen others will be described.

Because they cause fear for those who have not accumulated merit, who do not know their true nature, and who belong to the lineage of the Śrāvakas and so forth, they are called "terrifying" (bhayānakī).
As it was said by the noble Rāhulabhadra: "They appear terrifying to the ignorant."
Because it is the cause of hell for one who is perverted, who views through the superimposition of annihilation, and whose face is turned away from the paths to heaven and liberation, it is terrible;
as it is said in the *Abhayapaddhati*, the commentary on the *Śrībuddhakapālamahātantrarāja*: "One who does not see you is bound."
In some places, the reading is *ghora-ṣaḍgatī*; in that case, *ghora* refers to cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, this wisdom alone [is the same] for both these [beings] and others, regarding both cyclic existence and nirvāṇa.
As it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna: "The thorough understanding of cyclic existence itself is called nirvāṇa."

Thus, in the *Śrīsampuṭatantra*, the Vajra-holder has said: "The mind— overwhelmed by the darkness of manifold conceptualizations, flickering like lightning driven by the wind, and smeared with the stains of passion and other irresistible defilements— is indeed what he called *saṃsāra*."

The supreme being declared that very state to be the excellent nirvana: luminous, free from conceptual construction, and devoid of the stains of passion and other defilements; it is neither the grasped object nor the grasping subject.
Therefore, there is nothing beyond this that serves as the cause for the vast heap of suffering;
likewise, for those seeking liberation, there is nothing beyond this that serves as the cause for the arising of infinite bliss.

He indicates that cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) is possessed of great supernatural power (*maharddhika*) through the abundance of infinite bliss; [this is explained] starting from "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) and ending with "number.
"Conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) refers to various imaginings such as existence and non-existence, permanence and annihilation, the grasped and the grasper, and so forth.
This very volition, proceeding thus as a continuum,
demonstrates the means for attaining its arising and ceasing— that is, its production and cessation.
"Non-conceptualizing" means those things which are non-conceptual.
He asks: "Which ones? and replies: "Inferior," and so forth. "Inferior" refers to subtle objects consisting of mind and mental factors;
"superior" refers to everything down to children, because they are the objects of the conventional usage of entities (*bhāva*).

The gross-form entity is the embodied one itself; the intermediate is other than the two. Ālī and Kālī are thus the body, speech, and mind, designated by the terms inferior, intermediate, and superior as appropriate.
By the phrase "the others," which refers to the six sense-faculties, the stable elements such as earth and so forth, as well as other moving beings, are denoted.

The first chapter states in the *Hevajratantra*: "The inferior is the subtle object; the superior is said to be the state (*bhāva*); the middle is that which is devoid of the two; others are the six sense faculties; and those which are stable and moving. These [categories] beginning with the inferior are non-conceptual (*avikalpa*). When cultivated within the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), they become manifest as consisting of the innate (*sahaja*), but not by merely stretching out one's legs. Thus, by the word "non-conceptual," cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is indicated. Now, what is the meaning of "cultivation through the non-conceptual state"? The meaning is that cultivation is simply the non-contemplation of all phenomena by means of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) as the method.
Therefore, is the mental attention to great bliss (*mahāsukha*) neither faulty nor faultless?
Because it is not distinct from the entire world, and since the world is empty, it too is empty; thus, it is impossible to contemplate it.
The mental attention directed toward that [object] is taught as being "faulty" because it is conducive to non-reflection,
as it has been said: "Even through error, there is benefit, because another error is thereby dispelled."
Therefore, the thorough knowledge of all phenomena as being free from conceptual construction is itself designated as "cultivation" (bhāvanā) in its ultimate sense as a continuous process.
In this regard, whenever stability of mind occurs, at that very moment there is the yoga of meditative equipoise (samāhitayoga);

at other times, however, there is only the yoga of non-equipoise (asamāhitayoga). For this very reason, in the Stage of Arising (utpannakrama), the yoga of meditative equipoise is taught even without the yoga of the mudrā.
Because one abides through the means of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) by way of non-conceptualization regarding all phenomena, accomplishment (*siddhi*) arises precisely from the yoga of the mudrā.

Thus, in this scripture, she is the highly fortunate one who, through the fulfillment of her own welfare, brings about the welfare of others and bestows happiness upon all sentient beings; such is the conclusion.
"Thus"— that is, the two stages;
"with joyful eyes" means with eyes wide open due to the extreme joy arising from hearing about the generation stage and the completion stage.
"By that mind" means those with a conscious mind;
"those whose intellects are skillfully sharpened" refers to those proficient in the two stages; "by prostration" means having prostrated.
"For the sake of which" means that he has grasped the object to be established; "having grasped" refers to the words beginning with "atha" (now), and so forth.
The summarized meaning here is as follows:

that previously mentioned book, which issued from the skull of the Blessed One when Citrasenā entered his heart and rested there, was now—due to its being a mere mental appearance (*pratibhāsa*)—received from the hand of Vajrapāṇi. Having entered through the eyebrows for the sake of compilation, it became the *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the great king of tantras, the *Śrī Buddhakapāla*, which is the heart melted into fluidity;
therefore, the subsequent recitation (*saṃgīti*) is rendered possible.
Regarding "in the recitation" (jape), it is as previously explained;
regarding "by various means" (vividhaiḥ), this refers to place, time, and so forth;
and regarding "stobha, stambhana, and so on," these are those things which have been described.
In this regard, he clarifies the question—namely, how certainty arises concerning what is to be practiced and regarding the times of death—with the words "Which ones? and so forth;
"ka" means happiness, and that which protects (pālayati) happiness is "kapāla," which is indeed the lotus (*kāpāla*).
It is called "triangular" because it arises from three corners; it is the union of the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady, the Vajra and the Lotus.
Internally, however, the Vajra is the *bodhicitta*, and the Blessed Lord has arisen through the secret wheel (*guhyacakra*).
Because of the statement that "the Blessed One has the form of semen," the *kāpāla* [nature] exists because of its presence in the skull of *rajas*;
for this very reason, it arises from the triangular secret organ.
According to the instruction, the union of those two occurs through Ratnagarbha, Karmacāṇḍālī, and so forth;
however, in the ultimate sense, it is the union of the Buddha and the Kāpālika, that is, of emptiness and compassion.
Within the secret internal state of that union of the three realms, the avadhūtī channel, Citrasenā, resides as the primary [consort].
From its vibration, however, there arises even the seventy-two thousand channels (*nāḍī*).

Regarding the meaning of the word *citrasenā*, he says "wondrous" (*citram*): it is the cause of the wondrous qualities such as power (*bala*) and fearlessness (*vaiśāradya*), which are unobscured; it is emptiness endowed with the excellence of all aspects (*sarvākāravaropetā śūnyatā*). That itself is the army (*senā*), a multitude, because the triple world—consisting of the stable and the moving—is of the nature of the gnosis of great bliss (*mahāsukha-jñāna*). By this, the Blessed One is called *Buddhakapāla* due to the inseparability of emptiness and compassion.

Likewise, it is indicated by the Blessed Lady Citrasenā that those great beings go by means of that very vehicle; and since the Mahāyāna, consisting of cause and fruit, arises from the *cakra*, she calls it "Yoginī" because of its excellence through the threefold yoga.
The yoginīs and the channel that is the nature of the yoginī is the *avadhūtī*;

it arises through the aforementioned yoga. That very same divine gnosis which was previously mentioned becomes, through the sequence of the heat of meditation (*bhāvanā-uṣmā*) and so forth, the marvelous, great-divine fruit, the gnosis of Vajradhara.
"Bringing happiness to all sentient beings" is easy to understand.
Some read the text as "bringing happiness to all Buddhas"; in that case, it means bringing happiness to all the aggregates and so forth, which have the nature of a Buddha.
To the question "How is this so?", he says:

"Variegated," and so forth; this very great divine [deity] is established in the *kapāla* and *dharmodayā* according to the mantra and tantra systems, and thus the mantra begins with "Oṃ buddha... and so on.
And the Tantra, as previously described,
remains together with those two as stainless;
alternatively, Mantra is the single flavor of emptiness, which is great bliss.

Having shaken off conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) by means of the *tantra* (continuum) and its sequence, he remains established. "Born from the secret wheel" (*guhyacakreṇa sambhūtaḥ*) does not exist in the Sanskrit manuscripts; rather, the first chapter has been adopted according to the Tibetan version.

In that [chapter], it says "the triangle of that very skull-bowl" (*kapālasyaiva trikoṇam*); this is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) used because it performs the function of a triangle, in order to indicate that there is no other means.

"In that place" means where that divine gnosis (*jñāna*), which is of the nature of the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*), arises; and by relying upon which, through practice, that very [gnosis] occurs during the fourth consecration—
therein is the "place," namely the fourteen consecrations, five times seven.
Regarding the phrase "designating the Buddhas," we shall explain those [deities] such as Akṣobhya who are their purifications;
the various applications, such as the rites for pacification (*śāntika*) and so forth, will be explained below;
and [the rite for] increasing longevity.

That very gnosis, by virtue of mastery over life-span (*āyur-vaśitā*), or else, at the knot of the emanation wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*), is a subtle white drop endowed with five rays, having the nature of the five empowerments (*pañcābhiṣeka*) and denoting the seven Buddhas;
that drop is to be encircled by seven lines.
And those [energies], subtle and blazing, go out with the exhalations of the wind and enter with the inhalations; they enter together with the mind into the *bindu*.
Through such meditation, the innate gnosis (*sahajajñāna*) is born; this is the meaning of the "seven empowerments.

Regarding the phrase "increasing the lifespan," the instruction is that it occurs through the cessation of the entry and exit [of the breath] by means of the recitation whose nature is wisdom and method (*prajñopāya*).
He says that all of this is difficult to understand without the instruction of a guru:
"the path of instruction," meaning that instruction is the path, the specific means for it.
That is so;
and the instruction has been explained by us and will be explained further.
This concludes the first chapter in the *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the *Śrī Buddhakapāla-mahātantra*, composed by the scholar Abhayakaragupta.

The second chapter on mantras, titled "The Application of Alkali and the Determination of Various Rituals. He speaks this chapter on mantras in order to explain the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*).

Regarding the words "Now," and so forth: because the stage of generation consists of the embodiment of mantra, and because the expansion of ritual activity—which is a limb of the stage of generation—is accomplished through mantra, it is called "mantra. Mantra is the act of reciting, the invocation, and the exhortation to reality; thus it is declared.
I shall fully explain that chapter which elucidates it, as it was received from the Blessed One Vajradhara in the twelve-thousand-verse root tantra, the *Buddhakapāla*.
"Vajra" refers to the substance of the commitment (samaya-dravya); this is the mantra for its offering.
Since all accomplishments (siddhis) are preceded by the *bali* offering, he says:
"Oṃ Mahākapālavajra," and so forth.

Indra and the others, together with their retinues and all elemental beings (bhūtas), belong to this Blessed One; thus it is "sārvabhautika. Bali is a specific type of ritual offering. The mantra is that which presides over it.
The mantra for the *sārvabhautika* bali offering:

Here, in the ten directions, one should instantly visualize the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and so forth, as well as Indra and others with their retinues and immeasurable living beings, together with their wisdom and according to their respective degrees of superior wisdom, appearing in the forms of the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady; and one should offer them the bali—consisting of incense and other substances, composed of nectar, and resembling mercury—either by means of the visualization to be described or instantaneously. This is the traditional instruction (*āmnāya*).

Regarding "rice, namely *śāli*": a maiden who is unimpaired in her limbs and uninjured should wash the unbroken grains of *rakta-śāli* rice with white cow's milk. "Of the extremely fine" means *atyantasūkṣma*.
With that rice, ground in such a manner, one should have an effigy—a representation of Heruka—made;
one should make it oneself.
"Wise" means endowed with unimpaired wisdom.

"With the vajra-oil" means the vajra-oil produced at the time of the first menstruation of an intact maiden, which is the dual bodhicitta born from the vajra and lotus; this is mixed with *svayambhū* flowers.
Having ground [the ingredients] together with that, one should smear the effigy with an equal portion of powdered funeral pyre charcoal mixed with that.
By the yogins of Buddhakapāla, one should oneself manifest as the essence of Heruka in all applications.

Regarding the phrase "through the yoga of the form of Heruka": one should meditate upon the effigy—the *samayasattva*—as being non-different from the *jñānasattva*, as the actual Heruka himself. Thus, through the yoga of the effigy’s form as Heruka, having touched that effigy with one's hand, one should recite the mantra beginning with "Oṃ Mahāvajra" one hundred and eight times.
"Water" refers to vajra-water.
Thereafter, having bathed the effigy and worshipped it according to one's desired intention,
with that bathing water [one should perform] for oneself...
"There is none, O Lord!—
of the King,
O Lord!"
Second Chapter: By washing his face, the practitioner becomes invisible. He speaks of the application of alkali (kṣāra) with the words "of that" and so forth.
The phrase "pierced with the wood of the *babbūla* tree" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
"With fire" means with the fire of the cremation ground; "of that" refers to the *puktalaka*.
Regarding "with the Brahmavraja":
the Brahmavraja is Vairocana; "of that" refers to the effigy. "Kṣāra" means ashes. "With this" refers to [the mantra] beginning with *oṃ buddha* and so forth.
"Oṃ buddha," and so forth, ending with "adhiṣṭhaya hīḥ hūṃ," is one five-word mantra.
"Of the mantra" refers to the mantra itself. This is the traditional method (*sāmnāya*) here; it is the collective meaning.

In a cremation ground, having kindled a fire with the dry bark of *babbola* wood and dry *vairocana* wood, one should place that effigy—into whose heart the *babbola* wood has been inserted—within that fire. Then, into the heart of that effigy, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations with the five-word mantra beginning with "Oṃ Buddha," which is the *brahmavraja*.
Having burned that effigy, one should reduce it to ashes.

Thereafter, one should draw a four-petalled lotus in the center of an unbaked clay bowl or a lotus-vessel; on its wooden handle, one should write the word *citrasenā* from the five-word mantra, and the other words on the petals. Indeed, the deity, in the form of the mantra, is the accomplisher of all siddhis.

Thus, according to the statement in the *Siddhaikavīratantra*, one should meditate upon the intrinsic nature of one's own deity through the non-duality of the mantra and the deity. Then, having placed that alkali in an unbaked earthen bowl, one should consecrate it twenty-one times daily at the three junctions of the day with the mantra beginning "Oṃ buddha," one hundred and eight times each time. Following that, by doing the same for the skull-cup (*kapāla*), the alkali becomes perfected.
"By that"— meaning by the one thus established and crushed by Vajracūḍa—
"he himself" refers to the enemy.
He states the second application:
Having struck [the opponent] with the index finger while threatening him, one should rotate the thumb and cause it to fall face-down.
This explains the fourth application. "By that very same" means by that which has been accomplished.
That alkali, prepared and purified, along with an equal portion of tin powder (*vaṅga-cūrṇa*) and *vajracūḍa*—
where "a little" refers to the external measure of the tin powder—
all of this being mixed together; [one adds] the juice or blood of a black boar called *vajratuṇḍa*, or, according to the reading *vajradaṇḍa*, the juice of *vajradaṇḍa*, which is human urine.

Having infused it with that blood or urine, one should subsequently place a *pala* measure of it in a copper vessel suitable for piercing with thorns; then, having filled it with the essence of *vajratuṇḍa* or human urine, one should infuse it for seven days according to the commentary on the *Śrībuddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja*, titled the *Abhayapaddhati*.
Following that, one should grind it in that very same vessel together with "great bile," that is, human bile, for seven days.

The word *tataḥ* means that one should place [the substance]—having performed the preliminary saturation (*bhāvanā*) with the juice of the *vajratuṇḍa* and other substances—into an iron vessel, specifically a magnetized iron vessel (*ayaskāntaloha-bhājana*) weighing one *pala* and capable of being pierced by a thorn.
The word *saḥ* means that one should cast or place either the copper vessel or the iron vessel into the fire.

Someone says: "One should cast it onto a ground that serves as a site for continuous fanning of the flames and place it there for seven days. Another, however, says: "One should cast it, meaning one should cause it to circulate [within the fire]."
Then that copper vessel, gold vessel, or iron vessel becomes silver.
Others, however, say:

"Having extracted it" means that after first saturating it in some vessel with the juice of *vajratuṇḍa*, one should then extract it and perform saturation, rubbing, and placement in a copper vessel or an iron vessel; then, together with that copper or iron vessel, one should cast it into the midst of the fire as before.
However, when situated in the *āvartanaya* [position], one should cause the powder of *vaṅga* and the powder of *kāntaloha* to diminish.
The passage beginning with "sahasra" and so forth is easy to understand.
He states the fifth application:
With that very [substance] thus prepared, at dawn on an auspicious day, one should place that alkali upon the head of a young girl; Vajracūḍa should bathe her.
One should fumigate her while reciting the five-step mantra, using five types of incense and five lamps.
He states the sixth application:
having planted white mustard seeds— the fruit of the established doctrine— into the skull of a young girl, one should [use] the fruit produced from that,
consecrated seven times with this mantra after performing a preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) consisting of one hundred thousand recitations.
By that method of the *jyotiṣa*, empowered by all the Buddhas, the practitioner should recite the mantra while striking the mouth of a maiden or another woman.
Then that girl laughs.
"One" means that among the seven swords emerging from the mouth of the maiden, by suddenly seizing one sword, he becomes accomplished in the sword (*khaḍgasiddha*).
"Bhadraka" means one who is naturally disposed toward goodness (*bhadrikā-prakṛtistha*).
He states the seventh application (*prayoga*),
beginning with the words "of that," and so forth.

Having wrapped a pill of alkali (kṣāra) in gold and silver foil (tāra) respectively, one should subsequently empower it seven times with the Raukṣa mantra after reciting it one hundred thousand times; then, upon the appearance of heat, smoke, and flame, one should place it in the mouth.
In this regard, the measure of gold is three māṣakas plus seven and a half raktikās, and that of silver is four māṣakas plus two and a half raktikās.
Three māṣakas of gold, with an additional five raktikās, constitute the weight for the cord (śulva).
As it is stated in the second chapter: "Seven and a half, three and a half, four and a half;
five guñjās and three māṣakas are well-established for the binding of the pill."
"The mantra for accomplishing the three worlds" refers to the mantra for agitating the city.
The distinction between the colors of the Lord and the Lady according to their respective activities will be explained in the eighth [chapter].
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the *Śrī Buddhakapāla-mahātantra*, composed by the scholar Abhayākaragupta.

The third chapter: the consecration of the manifestation of the eight and three deities. Having explained the mantra, he speaks of the form consisting of mantra and the manifested form that is to be described, beginning with "atha" and so forth. "Devatāpaṭalam" means the chapter concerning the deities who have arisen from the class of mantras.
Regarding "by the syllable RAṂ," and so forth:
we shall explain clearly elsewhere the meditation on the mandala-circle as a whole.
Internally, however, it begins with "the vajra-ground," and so forth.

The vajra-ground is the navel; in its center, one should contemplate the syllable *E*, the Great Self whose nature is the *dharmadhātu*. One should visualize the triangular *dharmodaya* (source of phenomena), the *nirmāṇacakra* (emanation wheel) consisting of the three realms, which is the transformation of the syllable *E*.

In the center of that triangle is the seed-syllable *ekāra* or *laṅkāra*. From its transformation arises the earth-maṇḍala. In the heart is the syllable *vaṃ* or *oṃ*; it is the Dharma, the mind, its very self, and the wheel arising from it is the Dharmacakra.
"Having the nature of all channels" means having the essential nature of the eight channels.
Because even the channels of the four wheels are not distinct from the mind of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), they have that as their essential nature.
"The Yoginī is established in the head."

The thirty-two *yoginīs* are the thirty-two channels (*nāḍīs*) situated in the place of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), which, flowing and bringing forth the *bodhicitta*, abide there; that [place] is the divine wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) whose very nature they are.

Regarding these thirty-two channels, which are the nature of all channels, their common function is the bringing forth of *bodhicitta*; however, their specific functions and names should be stated according to other tantras.
Among them, *avadhūti* brings forth *bodhicitta* alone.
The *lalanā*, hanging from the base of the navel, brings forth essence (*rasa*) from the black and yellow [substances] cooked by the digestive fire (*jaṭharānala*).
Then, that essence pervades the body by circulating through various successive channels (*nāḍī*).
The *rasanā* brings forth blood from the essence.
Then that [wind] likewise pervades the body. This is a summary of all [the channels]:
the one carrying the nails and teeth is indestructible; the one carrying the hair of the head and body is subtle.
The divine Vāmā carries the skin and impurities, while [the other] carries the flesh.
Vasāvahā is Vāminī; Kūrmajāsthivahā is considered [to be] Matā; Bhāvakī carries the kidneys; Sekā carries the heart;
Doṣā is considered to carry the eyes; Viṣṭā is remembered as carrying bile.
The two mothers are the carriers of the lungs; Śarvarī is the carrier of the urine.
The third chapter: Śītā is in the lateral channel (pārśvatantre), Ūṣmā is that which carries [the wind] to the abdomen; Lalanā carries Akṣobhya, and Avadhūtī carries the Moon.
Rasanā is known as the carrier of blood and is considered to flow toward excrement;
Sīmanta has a black mouth and is common to both, carrying pus.
Hetu is said to be in phlegm; Viyogā is the carrier of sweat;
Premā is said to be in fat; and Siddhā is the carrier of tears of grief.
Pāvakī is considered to be in the nose, Sumanā is the carrier of snot; Trivṛttā is considered to be in form, while Kāminī is remembered to be in sound.
Gandhāvahā resides in the house, while Caṇḍikā is the giver of taste;
Yoginī is to be known by touch, and Māradārikā is in the wind.

Thus it is said. Here, Lalanā, Rasanā, and Avadhūtī are Citrasenā; the others, however, are in pairs respectively: Sumālinī, Kāpālinī, Bhīmā, and Durjayā. The remaining twenty, beginning with Śubhamekhalā, should be known as having the nature of Yoginīs. Māradārikā, however, being joined with Avadhūtī, rises from the navel to the tip of the tongue; this Kālanāḍī brings about the characteristic of restraint for the Dharmayoginīs.
That Yoginī enters by way of synthesis;
since she is of the nature of ignorance, how is it appropriate that she carries the thirty-two drops of bodhicitta in the second cycle?
There is no fault, because she carries them through the channel of time (*kālanāḍī*) by means of opposition.
However, in the context of the instruction on the channels that constitute the nature of the Yoginīs, that instruction is for the purpose of avoidance;
for it is solely due to their influence that this world does not perceive this maṇḍala, which is composed of great bliss even though it has arisen,
and it is solely due to their influence that one dies.
For this very reason it is said: "One should diligently abandon all remnants.
However, the Blessed One, the Vajra of Bodhicitta, is the means for all of them.

And this has been described as the Arisen Maṇḍala, which in the ultimate sense is the nature of Bodhicitta—inseparable from emptiness and compassion—arising even without the production [of deities] from seeds and so forth.
"Adorned with sixteen digits" means that at the throat, this wheel of enjoyment (sambhogacakra) consists of sixteen channels (nāḍīs).
"The emanation" refers to the lotus of emanation (nirmāṇapadma), which possesses sixty-four petals and channels therein.

"Thus" means that in the four wheels there are twenty-four channels; in the *Śrībuddhakapālamahātantrarāja-ṭīkā* titled *Abhayapaddhati*, it is stated that there are one hundred and twenty channels. "One should contemplate thus" means one should contemplate the arisen maṇḍala in this way;
one should meditate upon it and recite [the mantra].

In that regard, because the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) holds sovereignty over half-an-hour intervals within the *lalanā* and *rasanā*, there are sixteen transitions (*saṃkrānti*) in a single day and night at the throat. Furthermore, due to the division of the four mandalas and its sovereignty over four-hour periods (*daṇḍa*), there are sixty-four *daṇḍas* in the *nirmāṇacakra*.
As stated by the Blessed One in the *Saṃpuṭa* and other tantras, and by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna: "In the southeast, the northwest, the northeast, and likewise the southwest..."
Its movement within the maṇḍala consists of upward, lateral, and downward motion.

In that very [heart], from the enjoyment of the two mandalas consisting of wisdom and means individually, and from the movement through the network of channels, there are thirty-two channels in the wheel of great bliss;
and by the division of day and night and the distinction between wisdom and means, there are eight watches (praharas) in the heart.

In other tantras, that which is described as an *ahorātra* consisting of sixty *daṇḍas* is established here by means of the arrangement of *daṇḍas* according to three hundred and sixty breaths; however, here, by means of the arrangement of the four maṇḍalas, the establishment of the *daṇḍa* is by three hundred and thirty-seven and a half breaths. In both cases, there is no difference in that twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths constitute an *ahorātra*. Thus, with respect to the *utpannakrama*, the recitation (*jāpa*) is also indicated as being of the *utpanna* type.
As it has been said: "Two tens of thousands, one thousand, and likewise six hundred."
If the lord of yogis performs the recitation count within a single day and night.
When the mind of one who has recited the vidyā attains stability, the mandala consisting of great bliss (mahāsukha) becomes manifest.

"The wise one" refers to one who possesses superior wisdom and is skilled in the meditation on the mandala arisen from that [recitation]. In the "vajra-body"—that is, in the body consisting of great bliss which is of a single flavor with emptiness—one is a "great-souled one" (mahātman) because of being fit for the attainment of Mahāmudrā for both oneself and others.
"Therein" means in the wheel of dharma (dharmacakra).
In the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), the Varuṇa-maṇḍala is produced by the syllable *vāṃ*.

The statement "the entire network of channels (*sarvanāḍīmaṇḍala*) dissolves into the Varuṇa-maṇḍala" means that the emanation of the eight channels of the heart alone constitutes the other wheel of channels; therefore, the entire network of channels merges into the Varuṇa-maṇḍala.

"Again," and so forth: at the *nirmāṇacakra*, there is a blazing triangular fire-maṇḍala produced from the syllable *ma* or the syllable *raṃ*. It is joined to the *nirmāṇa*-channel-wheel. Below the fire is a wind-maṇḍala produced from the syllable *ya* or the syllable *yaṃ*.
Its nature is the movement of all the channels.

That wind-maṇḍala, kindling the fire, causes the *bodhicitta* situated in all the channels to move. Thus ends the third chapter. "The knower of the dissolving wheel": *vit* is the knowing (*vedana*) within the dissolving wheel.
When that aroused *bodhicitta* dissolves into the wheel of wind, then the experience of innate bliss (*sahajasukha*) occurs.
As all those [elements] dissolve, that yogi remains situated there in the center;
therein, within the experience of innate bliss, all the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth dissolve.
The yogi’s mind also abides as identical with that [energy];
"the moon" is the bodhicitta from the wheel of great bliss up to the crown protuberance (uṣṇīṣa),
and "the sun" is the *rajas* below the wheel of emanation (*nirmāṇacakra*).

In some places, the reading is *hū~ āḥ*; alternatively, it is *hū~ aṃ*. The syllable *hū~*, blue in color, is at the Dharma-wheel (*dharmacakra*); the syllable *āḥ* or *aṃ*, red in color, is at the Emanation-wheel (*nirmāṇacakra*).
In the saṃbhogacakra, there is a red syllable *oṃ*, according to the statement in another tantra;
it is "adorned with the letter *ka* and the letter *ha*," meaning it is both the letter *ka* and the letter *ha*, and it is adorned.

What is great bliss? Its nature is the syllable *Ha* in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), which is empty at its head, adorned with the unstruck sound (*anāhata*), the crescent moon, and the bindu; one should contemplate it as white. As for the syllable *Ka*, it dissolves into the syllable *Ha*; that is to say, great bliss becomes blended and non-differentiated within the unstruck sound.

*Ha hūṃ abhinnakam*: the meaning is that whatever is the nature of the unstruck (*anāhata*) sound, such is the nature of the syllable *hūṃ*; both possess the nature of both. For as it is said: "That bliss is remembered as the beloved woman. *Ka* is wisdom (*prajñā*) and *ha* is method (*upāya*); their non-duality is likewise the syllable *ha*, which is of the nature of bliss through its union with the syllable *oṃ*. Thus, the two syllables *ha* and *hūṃ* are mixed; *taṃ* and *hūṃ* are the mind and the method, representing the non-duality of wisdom and method.

"Regarding the phrase *hūṃkāraṃ raśmayaḥ* (the *hūṃ*-syllable as rays): impelled by the wind, the fire of Caṇḍālī is set in motion as rays and emerges from the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*). There, by the moon being impelled, the moon—which is like snow in its pacification of the fever of conceptual construction—merges with the *hūṃ*-syllable of great bliss; and by the sun, which is the passion (*rajas*) and the *haṃ*, they rest within the *oṃ* of the moist innate (*sahaja*). Then the *hūṃ*-syllable also melts and rests within the seed-syllable of emanation (*nirmāṇabīja*)."
And that [bindu] within the two mandalas of the moon and sun—the two mandalas having become mixed—is seen as the risen form of a drop (*bindu*), namely the solar dust-mandala (*rajomaṇḍala*) alone;
the semen (*śukra*), however, is unrisen.
Furthermore, there are the rays of the syllable *hūṃ*.
The syllable *hūṃ*, as a flowing drop (*bindu*) and a line of light rays, touches the entire wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*).
This is called the "seed" (*bīja*), and because it takes the form of a drop (*bindu*) at the arising of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), it is described as the "drop-yoga" (*binduyoga*).
Furthermore, in the meditation on the arisen maṇḍala, even the Caṇḍālī in the form of *rajas* spontaneously blazes up without the generation of the seed-syllable and so forth.
And the moon, ignited by that [fire], flows exceedingly; then the Caṇḍālī is meditated upon.

And the moon, intensely heated by that, blazes up exceedingly and flows even more. Thus, the internal union of the moon and sun is uninterrupted, consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*), [encompassing] the aggregates, elements, and so forth. By this, he states the necessity of receiving all the empowerments (*abhiṣeka*).
"In the state of Heruka" means:

What is the purpose of accomplishing [the deity] through meditation in the form of Heruka, given that Buddhahood cannot exist without initiation (*seka*)? The meaning is that it would result in nothing more than merit.
Regarding the word "that" (*sa*), because it is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the outer and secret initiations, the wisdom and fourth initiations are also to be understood as included.
The third chapter in the *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the *Śrī Buddhakapāla-mahātantra*, composed by the scholar Abhayākaragupta.
