3 | The fourth chapter, concerning the application of *śālikā* and the application of water, begins with "Now," etc., in order to speak of the *gārūḍa* [science of antidotes].
"By our ray"—the mantra that flashed forth in the first circle by means of the ray;
"the rays from the heart"—meaning the rays from Citrasenā's heart—having nourished the nāgas, returned and entered the heart of Citrasenā.
"Commanded"—meaning "we are the goddess," as the goddess said.

Citrasenā, having presided over the nāgas, put forward five questions through their spokesman for the purpose of explaining the reality of poison (*viṣatattva*). [The questions concern: what is the view regarding the *gāruḍa*—the mantra, medicine, and specific meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—of the outsiders (*tīrthika*) and others, such as Hari and Hara, as well as of the Blessed One Vajradhara;
what is the "source" (*sambhava*), meaning how that knowledge arises;
and what is the nature of this "arising of knowledge" (*jñānasambhava*).
The neuter gender [of *viṣasya*] is due to its being subordinate to the meaning of the qualifier.
"Of the poison" (*viṣasya*)—the question regarding the specific varieties is "What is the poison?
"They say" refers to the Nāgas.
"Harītyādi" and so forth; this is the answer to the fifth question regarding the position of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
In their view, Hari, Hara, and the others possess perverted intellects, as they are ignorant of the true nature of reality (*vastutattva*).
Fangs and fanged creatures, poison and death—these are the ultimate reality.

Therefore, due to their ignorance of the true nature of existence, sentient beings are afflicted by the defects of poison and die; they cannot even be revived by the *gāruḍa* [science of antidotes]. Thus they speak regarding one who has been bitten by Time (*kāla*).
[The calculation] is by means of the arrows (5), wings (2), seasons (6), fires (3), horses (7), pairs (2), and moons (1) for the day.
When sixty-six thousand seven hundred and ninety-nine years have elapsed.
"In the planetary hours (*vāra*), the times are half-praharas in due order; therein they say the fang is incurable. This is the answer to the third question.
They provide the answer to the first question:
"Of the serpent," and so forth.
If there is no Garuḍa-mantra (gāruḍa) for one bitten by Kāla, it "removes" [the poison], thus it is called *hara*; there exists a means of overcoming serpent venom composed by Hari, Hara, and others.
Such being the case, there is no antidote to serpent venom for one bitten by Kāla. The conclusion is that for one bitten by Kāla, there is no Garuḍa-mantra, and so forth.
They possess great supernatural power because they act as Garuḍas.
On the side of the Blessed One, they provide the answer to the second question,
beginning with "The Blessed One," and so forth.

He is the Teacher because he teaches what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. [The author] says "proponent of emptiness" to show that even those such as Hari and Hara are designated as "Teacher" by their respective devotees.

According to the maxim that "it is indeed difficult to explain that which is beyond perception, along with its goal and its cause," [the Buddha], having realized the true nature of all things, out of compassion—[as in the *Garuḍa*]—speaks of the essence of emptiness (*śūnyatātmatva*) to those disciples who are dependent on others.

"Certainty" (*niścaya*) means the state of being certain; it is an adverbial modifier of the action. (Note: The text fragment provided appears to be a commentary on a verse from the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*, specifically Chapter 9, Verse 2, regarding the difficulty of teaching the Dharma.)
The meaning is that Śaṅkara and others, being themselves uncertain regarding the reality, do not declare certainty for others either.
This was demonstrated in the response to the first question: that the meditative absorption on emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) alone is the unsurpassed remedy for poison.
"In the empty" means in those things devoid of intrinsic nature, because they lack a nature of being either one or many.

"That which is dependent origination is itself emptiness according to your view"—thus, regarding all phenomena, including the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), how could there not be a snake or the venom of its fangs? This means that when one has ascertained emptiness as the objective domain in this way, poison is necessarily destroyed. For this very reason, in response to the third question, [the Buddha asks] "How? and so forth. Regarding the fifth question, what is the meaning of the word "all" (*sarva*) in the phrase "in all cases"? The answer to the fifth question begins with "By the fang," and so forth.
They die because of their lack of certainty regarding emptiness;
therefore, the Blessed One speaks of certainty for them through discourse and teaching on emptiness.
Now, in order to state that [emptiness] is like the poison of snakes and so forth for those who have no internal poison, he says "rāga" and so on.
Attachment (*rāga*) is clinging to objects associated with the outflows (*sāsrava*).
Delusion (*moha*) is ignorance (*avidyā*), which is the insistence on existence, non-existence, and so forth.
"O Mahāyaśas" is an address to Citrasena.
"Those whose objects are mundane" (*prākṛtaviṣayāḥ*): here, "nature" (*prakṛti*) refers to ignorance (*avidyā*); those superimposed by that [ignorance] are "mundane.

Regarding "the objects of nature are perfectly stainless" (*prakṛtiviṣayasunirmalam*): here, "nature" refers to emptiness (*śūnyatā*); by means of that, the five objects—form and so forth—are thoroughly established within the mind along with their latent impressions (*savāsanam*).
Those for whom stains such as attachment have been uprooted and whose very nature is emptiness are "those [whose stains are thus removed]."
The use of the singular number for a plurality [of Buddhas] is due to their being *ārṣa* (sage-like); and their purity arises from the purity of the mind (*citta*). And the mind is pure by nature.
As it is said in the *Pramāṇavārttika*: "This mind is luminous by nature; the impurities are adventitious."
Thus [it is said].
He applies this to the present context with the words "the impurity," and so forth; the meaning is as follows:
passion and the like are themselves the internal poison.
As it was said by the Blessed One:
"Lust, hatred, and delusion—these three are the poisons in the world. And these are adventitious natures belonging to the mind alone.

Therefore, it is the mind itself—when deluded, attached, or hostile—that is the internal poison, because it destroys the life-force of the accumulations of merit and wisdom; and by the power of that mind, even the nature of sensory objects becomes poison.

However, when the mind is determined to be free from poison because its nature is inseparable from emptiness and compassion due to its purity, then how could even the nature of sensory objects, being free from defilement, ever be poison?
By this reasoning, it is indicated that one is not harmed by consuming stationary poisons and the like, provided there is resolute conviction in reality (*tattvādhimokṣa*).

This has been stated as an illustration in the *Hevajra Tantra*, in the fourth chapter, in the commentary on the *Śrībuddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja* titled *Abhayapaddhati*: "To whomsoever poison is food and the world is not an object of aversion;
whose mind is free from delusion—that person rejoices in the supreme reality."
Thus it is said.

Here, "free from delusion" means through the thorough knowledge of the reality of poison; "with a mind intent on the conviction regarding the reality of that very poison" means having a mind resolved upon the true nature of that poison.
That is the *aśoka* (the sorrowless); and therein, the destruction of internal poison is stated as the illustrative example. Likewise, those who know the means to cessation (*nirvṛti*).
"Those who have well-performed their labors in Hevajra are not afflicted by ignorance and the like, nor by the bonds of delusion and so forth.
Here, "in Hevajra" refers to the non-dual gnosis in which emptiness, great bliss, and non-referential great compassion are inseparable.

By means of the twelve factors beginning with ignorance (avidyā) and the afflictions (kleśa) such as delusion (moha), [the text] states that for one who is thus free from internal poison, even external poison does not cause harm. They explain the fourth question with the words, "Even a serpent... and so forth.
"Natural poison," "snake poison," and likewise "defect. Nature (*prakṛti*) is ignorance; that which arises from the superimposition thereof is "natural poison" (*prākṛtam viṣam*).
This belongs to the snake, hence it is "snake [poison]" (*sarpaviṣam*); there is no increase of the vowel *a* due to the absence of the suffix *aṇ*.
The connection is: "What will both the object (*viṣaya*) and the poison (*viṣa*) do?
This is the answer to the second question regarding the position of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*):
"The gods are obstructed by objects."

Śaṅkara and others, whose knowledge of reality has been obscured regarding sense objects by the afflictive and cognitive obscurations, possess both internal and external poison. Nevertheless, due to their great power, they act as Garuḍas and claim that the state of being bitten by the fangs of Time is something to be overcome.
Therefore, he will say:
"one who is devoid of intellect yet possesses great supernatural power.

The Blessed One Buddhakapāla, however, demonstrates that one whose latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) have been uprooted and who is free from all obscurations (*āvaraṇa*) enjoys sensual pleasures and yet is not afflicted by them.
"Objects," and so forth.

Thus, even while engaging with all sense objects, the practitioners of the Buddha-Kapāla yoga do not become defiled; for they are untainted by virtue of their yoga with the Buddha-Kapāla. He says "Buddha," and so forth.
They conclude by way of including all [the remaining] characteristics.
"Then from Kāladaṃṣṭra" refers to the yoga of Buddhakapāla.
Having thus explained the ultimate Gāruḍa, they state the conventional one.

The meaning is that the *śālikīs* and others—meaning the non-Buddhist heretics (*tīrthikas*)—who are self-restrained in this practice of *śālikīkaraṇa*, declare that Kāladaṃṣṭra is incurable, whereas the Blessed One says he is not.
Having spoken thus, the nāgas prostrated before Citrasenā and departed for their respective abodes; so it is said.
The compiler [states] "such as this" and so forth.
"Imagination" (utprekṣā) is the definition of its essential nature.
"Oṃ" refers to body, speech, and mind.

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the absence of intrinsic nature (*naiḥsvabhāvya*), primordial wisdom (*jñāna*), and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*)—these three, being indivisible, constitute the vajra-nature. I am he whose self-nature is that [vajra-nature]. Just as I am thus the fourth chapter, so too is "all" (the universe); thus it says, "the name of emptiness. It is empty because it is devoid of its own inherent form;
yet it is not empty because it is nevertheless inexpressible.
And because it abides in a form devoid of duality.
"Five spans" refers to a square mandala measuring sixty finger-breadths (aṅgulas) on each side, located within the root-line;
the circular [mandala] measures thirty finger-breadths.
Right there, one should prepare an eight-petaled lotus, thirty finger-breadths in size, encircled by a row of blue vajras.

In other tantras, purification through digging the ground and removing impurities (*śalya*) is taught; however, because this is a superior tantra, it is said that one should purify the site for the maṇḍala and the site for the fire-pit (*homakuṇḍa*) to be described later by touching it with the hand and reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times.
Regarding the passage beginning with "bhūmi" and so forth:
here, he states that in the mandala pertaining to the Gāruḍa section, the altar (vedi) and the platform (paṭṭī) need not be constructed.
This is expressed in the passage beginning with "vedikā" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "with red powder," one should fill the entire area of the mandala in the four directions with red-colored powder alone.
He states that it is not as there is a differentiation of colors for the ground according to the specific directions of Vairocana and the other [deities] in the *Samāja* and other [tantras],
by saying "here" and so forth.
One should fashion the other [mandala] with five lines and so forth, using powders of five colors as appropriate.

The offering of oblations (*balidāna*), the purification of the ground, the marking with the thread (*sūtramantraṇa*), and the casting of the colored powders (*rajaḥpātādi*) with the thread must be performed by a Guru who possesses the yoga of Heruka.
Regarding the "vases" (*kalaśā*):

In the four jars located in the corners, beginning with the northeast (īśāna) and southeast (āgneya), there are four symbols respectively: those with roots at the wrong time, elongated bellies, and thick lips, and those with long necks. Although the fifth, the Vijaya jar, is not explicitly mentioned here for the central deity, it should be understood according to the principle of other tantras as being placed slightly to the south of the eastern door.
That very [mandala] here is the one for all rites.
In that regard, the sign is a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) in the center of the source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*).
The hand-drum is surrounded by a vajra and a lotus.
The preceptor should be one who possesses the yoga of Buddhakapāla.
To explain how this is so,
he says "padma" and so forth.
In the pericarp of the universal lotus;
"afterwards," and so forth.
The Master himself, surrounded by the eight goddesses and having become the nature of Heruka, should consecrate himself immediately after the entry of the gnosis-being (jñānasattva).
Regarding the phrase "the rays from the limbs of Heruka":
the preceptor should cause the Tathāgatas to be touched by the eight goddesses who have radiated forth rays of light from the eight channels of the heart.
Those goddesses, having arrived, along with the goddesses emitted from the rays of the Tathāgatas, bathe the Lord Heruka and the eight Yoginīs.
"Adorned with a crown" means that Heruka is crowned, and together with the yoginīs, they too are adorned with crowns. "The completion of the maṇḍala" means:

thus, having oneself become the essence of Heruka, once the powder maṇḍala is completed, one should quickly visualize the pledge-being (samayasattva) and the gnosis-being (jñānasattva), as well as the consecration and sealing, through the practice of the maṇḍala.
"Food" (*bali*) refers to [offerings] for the *nāgas*;

"lamp" (*dīpa*) refers to honey, ghee, fish, ten-finger-breadths of oil, fragrant oil, and lamps—these four one should cause to be offered near the mandala. There are also four fruits: mango, coconut, plantain, and wood-apple (*kapittha*). [This concludes] the commentary on the great king of tantras, the *Śrī-Buddhakapāla*, titled *Abhayapaddhati*.
The three garments are the lower robe, the upper cloak, and the head-wrap.
The Yoginī herself offers the Guru’s consort.
The Hero, the Guru, the Cakra, and the assembly of the Gaṇas.
"With a mind focused solely on the essence of the commitment (samayasāra)" means that the Blessed One is the essence of the commitment. "The warding off of self-doubt" [is as follows].
The meaning is that poison becomes effective through fear, but not for one who is free from fear.
"Stationary" refers to poisons such as those from the *śṛṅgī* plant;
"mobile" refers to those of serpents and the like.
I render poisonless the fourfold poison: that which is born of living beings, such as *vicoḍikā* and the like; and that which is artificial, such as honey, ghee, and so forth.
"Wood" refers to the tooth-stick.
One should visualize the disciple as the form of Heruka.
"In the throat" refers to [the throat] of both the master and the disciple.
And in the left hand;
"in the moon" means [the mantra] located at the throat and located in the hand.
Since the visualization is possible, while visualizing Heruka’s form, the moon, and so forth, one should place the hand—thus visualized—upon the head of the disciple and recite the mantra.
"Kumbha" refers to the measure of a jar;

"duḥsaha" refers to suffering. Regarding the passage beginning with "gāruḍa," it means that when this being practices the Gāruḍa [mantra], then we shall have no recourse whatsoever as a refuge for protection.
"Immediately after" (anantareṇa) means immediately following the acceptance (adhivāsanā).
"Anudatta" is used in the sense of the agent; it is stated in the present tense due to its archaic (ārṣa) nature.
The meaning is that one should give them in sequence.
Regarding "conch-shell" and so forth: in one small box there is a conch-shell;
in the second, a copper vessel.
The *kalaśa*, the *vijaya-kalaśa*, and the other four *kalaśas*—
having become liquefied as the eight *yoginīs*—
abide in identity with the Blessed One and the deities situated within the maṇḍala.
The establishment of the mandala occurs precisely through the state of becoming of one flavor between the Samaya-being and the Wisdom-being.

One should contemplate the Victorious Vase as the Blessed One, with the eight goddesses having entered into it as liquid mercury, and in the other vases, one should contemplate the goddesses according to their respective positions.
Regarding "water": one should place a small amount of water from the *vijaya-kalaśa* and other vessels into a copper vessel and a conch shell.

Regarding "with water": first with the copper water, and subsequently with the conch water; with these two, the preceptor (*ācārya*) should cause the disciple to recite [the mantra] and have him read it. The Guru should worship the disciple. Regarding "in the disciple": when the blindfold (*andhapaṭa*) has been torn away.
The word "again" (punar) refers to the act of sprinkling; with both hands holding vajras,
one should cause [the disciple] to drink the water mixed with copper-vessel water from a conch shell while reciting the Heruka mantra three times.
He will explain the benefits of drinking water;
this is the sequence here:

the preceptor, having been duly consecrated by his gurus, skilled in the three samādhis, with the nature of Heruka, and having recited the vidyā-mantra, desires to consecrate the disciples who have been continuously and thoroughly examined and who are making their request.

First, in a maṇḍala house or similar location free from all disturbances such as kings and thieves, one should consecrate the ritual vases upon a powder maṇḍala or a cloth maṇḍala prepared according to the rules, where lamps have been offered as prescribed, the fivefold offerings beginning with fruit have been presented, and milk has been set out for the sake of the nāgas.

There, one should prepare the Victory Vase (*vijayakalaśa*), which is filled with scented water, situated in the center of a *dharmodaya*, marked with a *ḍamaru*, a vajra, and a lotus; it is filled with the five jewels—gold, lapis lazuli, pearl, coral, and emerald—and the five grains—barley, wheat, sesame, black gram, and rice; it is endowed with the five medicinal herbs along with their goddesses: *vṛhatī*, *kaṇṭakārī*, white *aparājitā*, blue *daṇḍotpala*, and *saha*; its mouth is adorned with mango sprouts, its neck is wrapped in red cloth, it is garlanded, its top is marked with a vajra, and above it stands a vessel filled with milk; having thus prepared it, one should visualize the *samayasattva* instantaneously arisen within it.

From the *hūṃ* seed-syllable situated within the Sun-Vajra Fist, one should summon the Blessed One, surrounded by the eight yoginīs, from the Marīci-niṣṭhā [realm]. Having recited the heart mantra seven times for the purpose of invitation, one should offer [the water] with the mantra: *oṃ heruka vajrārghaṃ pratīccha hūṃ*. Having caused him to enter into the midst of that [water], one should contemplate that water as being of the nature of bodhicitta consisting of great bliss (mahāsukha), having become one with the Samayasattva. Then, holding a garland of flowers with the left fist as a vajra, one should consecrate it one hundred and eight times with the heart mantra.

One should prepare the vases for the outer mandala, completely filled with scented water, joined with mango sprouts, their necks wrapped in red cloth, adorned with garlands, and marked respectively with the signs of the skull-cup (*kapāla*), the *khaṭvāṅga*, the knife (*kartti*), and the hand-drum (*ḍamaru*). Internally, they should be joined with the liquid of the Wisdom Goddess (*jñānadevī*), who is non-different from the Samaya Goddess (*samayadevī*). Each vase should be consecrated one hundred and eight times with the seed-mantra of its respective goddess. Among them, Śauṇḍinī and Citrasenā are associated with the skull-cup.
Bhūtinī is marked by a *khaṭvāṅga* on the Saubhadra [day]; the two four-armed goddesses dwelling in Pātāla are marked by a *kartṛ*; the two lovers dwelling in Ākāśa are marked by a *ḍamaru*.
HŪṂ OṂ HŪṂ SVAḤ HŪṂ KHAṂ HŪṂ HŪṂ are their seed-syllables (*bīja*) in due order.

Thereafter, having worshipped with flowers, incense, and so forth by the entire assembly, and having offered the *bali* oblation, the master—preceded by praise with the verse beginning "The lotus and the vajra"—should ring the bell and prostrate.

Immediately following the ritual procedure for the consecration of the vase (*kalaśādhivāsana*), the master, adorned with the three cloths and other ornaments provided by the disciple, accompanied by his consort (*prajñā*), and wearing a garland of *kelima* flowers, sits upon a seat outside the site of the mandala.

Having mentally caused the disciple—who has performed the triple-circle rite (*trimaṇḍala*), holds a flower garland, placed his knees upon the ground, joined his palms in *añjali*, and is auspiciously adorned with the *gāruḍa* [ornaments]—to enter his own body, [the master] emerges as Vajra and remains in the space of wisdom (*prajñā*). Then, having been consecrated by the melted Tathāgatas brought forth by the rays from the seed-syllable in the heart and entered through the *avadhūtī*, [the disciple] takes the form of Heruka. Seated at the eastern gate of the maṇḍala, he says: "O Blessed One, Teacher, solely intent on the welfare of sentient beings, I desire the divine *gāruḍa* born of the yoga of the *śālikā*."
"I shall perform the divine swallowing of those bitten by the Time-Snake for the sake of sentient beings;
tell me that, O Great Teacher, [you who are] the yogin of Buddhakapāla."

Having thus requested entry with these words, [one recites]: "The Three Jewels are my refuge; I confess all my misdeeds; I rejoice in the merit of the world; I direct my mind toward the awakening of a Buddha. This is the *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the *Śrībuddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja*.

Having thus caused [the disciple] to recite this three times, and having protected him with the heart-mantra, one should visualize the syllables HŪṂ—black, on the pericarp of a black vajra in his heart; ĀḤ—red, on a red lotus at his throat; and OṂ—white, on a white wheel at his head.

Then, having risen, while reciting *hūṃ āḥ oṃ*, one should touch the heart, throat, and head with the right fist joined with scented water and a vajra; then one should offer a flower on the head, incense and a lamp before [the deity], and perfume at the heart.

Following that, facing north, one should give a tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) made of *aśvattha* or other such wood—unbroken at the tip, straight, and measuring twelve finger-breadths—with its tip encircled by a garland of flowers, washed with fragrant water, and consecrated seven times with the mere mantra of the tooth-stick itself.
The disciple, having eaten from the front on ground smeared with the measure of a cow-hide, should cast it away without looking back, facing either east or north; thereafter,
for the purpose of sipping water (ācamana), he should drink three handfuls of scented water.
With this mantra, "Oṃ hrīḥ, O Pure Dharma, purify all the sins of this person and remove all conceptual constructions, hūṃ," one should perform [the rite].

Thereafter, the preceptor should visualize a moon-maṇḍala in his own left hand—which is smeared with fragrance and adorned with flowers—and at his throat; he should then imagine that the Buddhas of the ten directions are summoned by its rays, and having melted through great passion (*mahārāga*), they enter into the two moons.
Then, having placed that hand upon the head of the disciple, one should recite the adhivāsana mantra seven times.

Then, reflecting that the Buddhas residing in the throat and in the hands enter the body of the disciple together with the moon and perform an empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), one should protect the disciple.
Having spread out kuśa grass consecrated by the heart-mantra for the purpose of a bed, one should give it to him.

The master, having entered the maṇḍala house, should perform meditation and recitation. The disciple, having performed the rite of consecration (adhivāsana), should offer the bali offering at dawn, exit the maṇḍala house, and ask the disciple about his dream; he should then protect him with the heart-mantra. Having performed worship in the maṇḍala house according to his means, and having mentally honored the circle of deities as if they were actually present there by regarding them as his own guru, the master himself should first enter the maṇḍala according to the procedure for the entry of the disciple about to be described, completing everything up to the initiation (abhiṣeka) through his own family lord (kulādhipa). Then, having obtained permission from that very source for all the duties of a master, he should perform the empowerment of truth (satyādhiṣṭhāna).

O you who face the east! O all phenomena! O fourth chapter! By that truth through which true gnosis—the maṇḍala whose nature is wisdom and means—is attained; by that truth through which you fulfill the aims and desires [of beings];
phenomena are like reflections, transparent, pure, and untroubled.
They are ungraspable and inexpressible, yet they arise from causes and karma.
"By the truth that suchness has emerged from reality, may the disciples, free from all defilement, clearly behold the entire mandala as a reflection. Thus.

Thereafter, having bathed the disciple and rendered him pure with fragrant substances and the like, he should be clothed in a lower garment and upper robe of dyed red cloth, and his own face should be bound with a tied red cloth while he is visualized in the form of Śrī Heruka. With the mantra *āḥ khaṃ vīra hūṃ*, he should be made to hold a flower; having been given a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) outside the curtain (*kāṇḍapaṭa*), sprinkled with water from the all-purpose vase (*sarvakarmika-kalaśa*), and stationed at the eastern gate of the mandala by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, the master should ask him for the purpose of entering the mandala: "Who are you?
To which he should reply:

Then, thinking "I am a son of the Jina," one should generate the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) with the mantra: *oṃ sarvayogacittam utpādayāmi*. Then, holding a vajra with flowers at the heart, one should establish it while reciting: *oṃ surate samayas tve hoḥ siddhyatha vajra yathāsukham*. Thereafter, one should place the vajra upon the head and say: "This is your samaya-vajra; it shall split your head if you speak of this to anyone."
Then, having placed the vajra in the heart, one should speak thus:
"Oṃ! Vajrasattva himself is now established within your heart;
he will depart at that very moment, piercing through, if you should speak of this method."

Having thus caused [the disciple] to take the oath, one should recite seven times over the milk placed in a lotus vessel—situated atop a flask, mixed with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) empowered by the three syllables—the mantra *oṃ pañcāmṛtodaka ṭhaḥ hūṃ*. [One should say: "This is the water of hell; it shall burn you if you transgress the pledge (*samaya*)."
Reciting, "The accomplishment is the protection of the essence of the samaya; drink the water of vajra-amṛta," he should cause [the disciple] to drink it, saying:
"'Sāra' (essence) does not exist, O Bhagavān!
Hūṃ! O Bhagavān!"
"O Blessed One, having said, 'I must not be disregarded by you, lest your samaya be violated and you fall into the states of hell and so forth,' [the master] joins his palms in reverence.
Then he says: 'This disciple has been properly initiated into the mandala by me;
may he possess the lineage of the deities according to his merit. May whatever siddhi be his, and in whichever family he is a vessel.'"
"May her maṇḍala be such as the power of her merit.

Having made this *satyādhiṣṭhāna* (empowerment by truth), one should recite: "Oṃ Heruka Vajra, accept this flower, hūṃ," while throwing the previously taken flower—empowered with the syllable *trāṃ* and [held] with the syllable *hūṃ*—into the center of the maṇḍala using the five-syllable mantra.

Tying that thrown flower to the head of the disciple, one should recite: "O Great Hero, please accept this! Thereafter, having visualized the Lord upon the moon at the disciple's heart, the letter *ra* on the forehead, and two *oṃ*s on the two eyes, one should say: "Oṃ! Vajrasattva himself, intent today upon opening your eyes, opens for you the unsurpassed Vajra-eye of all vision."

Having removed the face-cloth while reciting, and having worshipped the ninefold mandala with incense and other offerings using mantras such as "Oṃ Heruka Vajra Puṣpaṃ Pratīccha Hūṃ," and having uttered "O Vajra, look! (he) should show the mandala after first pronouncing the names of the deities.
Following the procedure for entering the mandala, the disciple should prostrate with the five limbs, place his right knee upon the ground, and [offer] with palms joined in the *kapota* gesture.
I am submerged in the mire of saṃsāra; O refuge, be my protector!
I am dull-witted and devoted to other things, having been deprived of the Buddha's Dharma.

"O Lord, have mercy! O Lord, Teacher, Great Guru!"—with this recitation, one should perform worship. Then the Ācārya [thinks]: "At the time of bathing with the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdbīja*), let the compassionate ones bathe this [disciple] with the melted nectar produced by the blazing Caṇḍālī at his own navel, by means of the eight channels (*nāḍī*) emerging from the heart—the deities whose nature they are—and together with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and the Vidyā-devis, drawn forth by the rays of the heart-seed syllable. With palms joined, he should entreat them, prostrating again and again. Thus worshipped, [he recites]: *Oṃ vajraheruka...* [End of Chapter Four].

Accompanied by banners, flags, garments, musical instruments, and the like, and holding in their hands jars filled with the water of auspicious knowledge while singing auspicious songs, they consecrate the disciple who has taken the form of Heruka. At that very moment, having filled a copper vessel and a conch shell—both placed upon two small stands—with the water from the *vijaya-kalaśa* and other vessels, one first performs the consecration using the copper vessel held in both hands together with a vajra and a small amount of water, followed by the conch shell, [reciting]:
"I bestow the Great Vajra, honored by the three realms, which arises from the abode of the secrets of all Buddhas."
Reciting, "Oṃ, O hero Heruka, I consecrate you," while performing the consecration, one should cause the disciple to undergo the empowerment of the crown (*mukuṭādhiṣṭhāna*).
Then, having thus consecrated the disciple with both the water and crown empowerments, one should have him drink the remaining water— mixed with the residual water from the conch vessel—
three times while reciting the mantra beginning with "Oṃ Buddha," as stated in the first chapter.
"Preparations" refers to artificial [poisons];
others are vegetable poisons produced from limbs, such as *lāṅgalī* and so forth, as well as secondary poisons (*upaviṣa*).
*Kāṇḍaviṣa* means poison-water;
*lepana* refers to those poisons which, having been applied as ointments to food and other such items, are intended for consumption and so forth.
*Ye* (which) refers to those poisons.
"Those" means all of them;

"right there" means by those who have been bitten or given [the poison] right here, and by the act of making *śālikā*. If you desire merely the making of *śālikā*, then you are informed at that very moment; otherwise, it refers to the *Gāruḍa* [science], which is both worldly and ultimate—this is the meaning.
"Among a thousand," and so forth: within a thousand or a hundred, one should give the instruction to be described hereafter regarding the mantra to one of pure intention.
"To the serpent-biter," and so forth: "likewise" means without effort;
this is the meaning.
As long as another practitioner of the *gāruḍī* mantras performs or will perform rituals regarding the fangs, the yogin of the *Buddhakapāla* must not feel anxiety; rather,
once the other *gāruḍī* practitioners have abandoned the fangs, thinking, "This is Kāladaṃṣṭra, he is dead," the ritual should be commenced with the rays and so forth.

A ray of light from the seed-syllable of one’s own self in the form of Heruka was sent to the world of the *nāgas*, such as Vāsuki, drying up the heart of the *nāgas*. To the *nāgas* who were saying, "What shall we do?", he says, "Previously," which reminds [the reader] that in the first chapter here as well, she spoke as Buddhakapālinī; the sense is that you, overcome by the rays of the mantra, informed the Blessed Lady and accepted her command.
Therefore, it is said, "it became so," meaning that the practice was not properly performed.
"So be it," said the Nāgas.
"Go, Raśmi! For no bite has been seen by Kāladaṃṣṭra, nor is there any other fang-bearer besides Kāladaṃṣṭra."
The *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the *Śrī Buddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja*, states: "They do not die from the poison of doubt because of the removal of that doubt;
'raśmi' means rays of light; 'apatita-gomaya' is the dung of a tawny cow."
With that [substance], one should fashion a male *śālika* bird and a female *śālikī* bird;
one should make a white *aṣṭikā* from flour and white rice, place those two birds upon it,
and place within it a conch or other white vessel containing the soot from extinguished charcoal.
With that white oleander pen, one should write the mantra upon the heart of a *śālika* [bird], whether it be a female or a male; thus, a female *śālika* is a *strīśālikī*, and its male is a *śālika*.

However, because of this specific distinction, it is indicated that one should place the two leaves—such as birch bark (*bhūrja*) and so forth—upon which the written mantra is inscribed, into the heart of the male *śālika* and the heart of the female *śālikī*.
"One should cause ink to be prepared," and so forth;

having painted two rice-grains with that ink and placed them directly in front of one's own eyes, while looking at them as if they were two real rice-grains, one should recite the mantra seven times with a sprig of white karavīra and contemplate [the object] as non-different from the two divine rice-grains that have been invoked.
The single mantra beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *svāhā* has entered; having gone to those two rice-fields, it has entered the realm of the nāgas.
When the nāga Daṃṣṭra saw the great power of the rice-field [mantra], he thought, "If [the practitioner] does not die..."
The blind man will become one again;

Śālikā said to Śālikadvaya: "O Chest, speak these words—the words of accepting Citrasena’s command—and do not act otherwise. If the reading is "mākuruṣva," then the meaning is: since the King of Birds, Garuḍa, has caused all the birds of great power to observe a vow for the sake of protecting the Nāgas from harm through Jīmūtavāhana, you must not act contrary to that vow.

"Thus," and so forth: having grasped the head and tail with two stalks of *śāli* rice, [the practitioner] brings the intended object before the tip of the fang. After consecrating it with the snake-invocation mantra (*āvāhana-mantra*), he strikes with clay from a snake's burrow while reciting the invocation mantra. From the eye—where the fang was seen—the [mantric power] travels from the feet to the head, or from the head to the feet, three times. That [power] "pierces" (*ucchiti*) the fangs; then, having led the snake back to its own place along with the two stalks of *śāli*, one should always establish it in its own place once it has returned. This is the collective meaning. As for the individual meanings: "of what is grasped" (*gṛhītasya*) means those which have been grasped.
A snake dies by [the bite of] a snake; thus, his [body] has died and fallen.
"Gati" means movement as far as the head; "caraṇa" means movement as far as the feet.
He speaks of the conventional *gāruḍa*—which is the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*)—as being beyond the ultimate (*muktapāramārthika*). He then explains that very [knowledge].

"Empty," and so forth: empty means devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Having worshipped with devotion the Vidyā arisen from the five colors.
"Regarding the consumption of feces, urine, semen, blood, and so forth,
tell me now another divine rule, my child, according to your desire."
He too might think: "Why should I not be able to perform the rites, such as the observances (*samaya*) and so forth, exactly as the Goddess has commanded?
Why should I not have devotion? Why should women not always perform the worship of Padma?"—and thus he would accept [the practice].
Then, having caused the lotus to blossom, she should say, "Enjoy liberation! Hoḥ!

He too, having understood the distinctions such as bliss (ānanda) through the instruction of the Guru, should take delight in the place of pressure between the jewel and the pericarp within the space of the lotus.

Visualizing that mind as the vajra-paryaṅka posture extending to the tip of the jewel, that gnosis arises which is of that very nature. It is neither passion nor dispassion; the middle state is not perceived. Precisely through the avoidance of these three, it is called the co-emergent awakening (*sahaja-saṃbodhi*).
O friend, even though the luster of the body has dissolved and the senses have vanished, ask clearly about the state of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) while the Guru’s power remains;
as long as the yogi does not release the *bodhicitta*, he attains an uninterrupted, indescribable bliss born of joy.

But when the *bodhicitta*—the treasury of all accomplishments—has fallen, and the consciousness of the aggregates has fainted, from where could there be any irreproachable accomplishment? *The Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the *Śrī Buddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja*.

Having held it for as long as possible and then slowly releasing it, one should take up the *bodhicitta* in the form of the *samaya* from the lotus with the tongue while maintaining the vision of reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*).
Thereafter, she places her left hand on his head and gives her authorization. Then the Guru says:

"From this day forward, my son, until you reach the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), act for the benefit of all sentient beings with your whole being, as if in a dream. This is the wisdom of insight (*prajñājñāna*).
"Buddhahood is not attained by any other means than this vidyā. "O child, practice the vow of the vidyā, the highest of all vows. Thus he would speak regarding the vidyā-vow.

Thereafter, for the disciple who has indeed received the wisdom-knowledge (prajñājñāna), the guru should grant the fourth empowerment through speech alone—the fourth being the form of Vajradhara—based on the practice of that very wisdom-knowledge, as a specific point to be understood from the guru’s instruction.

This has been stated in the *Śrīsampuṭa*: "Having bestowed the initiation according to the prescribed rites and having mentally examined the disciple's inclination (*adhimukti*), one should bestow the jewel of initiation with words alone for one who is inclined toward the vast and profound method. This is the fourth initiation.

As for the disciple of middling faculties, one should visualize outside [the body]—within the interior of the lotus of the *dharmodayā*, which is the nature of cultivated wisdom—a mind-made triple-layered mandala measuring ten million *yojanas*, and then confer initiation upon him according to the appropriate procedure as described.

That disciple who, through the power that has arisen, clearly perceives these two maṇḍalas created by the Guru—who is himself an accumulation of merit—is one of the sharpest faculties (*adhimātrādhimātrendriya*). One should likewise confer initiation upon him. However, for one of dull faculties (*mṛdvindriya*), [initiation should be conferred] either in a powder-maṇḍala (*rajomaṇḍala*) or a cloth-painting-maṇḍala (*paṭamaṇḍala*); this instruction has been explained in detail out of fear of the loss of the oral tradition (*āmnāya*). The sixth chapter, concerning the stage of generation (*utpattikrama*), concludes with the description of the maṇḍala. Now, in order to describe the maṇḍala of the perfected state (*niṣpanna*), he says "kahiṃ" and so forth.
"Kahiṃ" signifies, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the negation of a foundational support (*ādhāra*).
The syllable *ka* signifies the prohibition of the form of a deity to be meditated upon.

Even if practices such as drawing mandalas are paths toward great enlightenment because they are means for accumulating merit, he says "in another place" (*pāntara*) to indicate that they are nevertheless distant from and empty of qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*).

He feels compassion for the world, which has fallen into the snare of "falsehood"— that is, into the nature of delusion, into conceptual superimpositions, and into the various distractions of the "garland of flowers" that obstructs the attainment of swift awakening and liberation.
Regarding "empty," and so forth, he asks:
how is that which has arisen as such—consisting of the aggregates and so on—[described as] "not other"? He says:
"Kamale" and so forth: the host of yoginīs situated within the lotus of great bliss (mahāsukha) has the nature of the channels (nāḍī). Heruka is the bodhicitta;

he himself is the essence of great bliss, whose single flavor is emptiness, and whose nature is like a dream, a reflection, or an illusion. He is said to have his origination in the form of the aggregates (skandhas) and so on; thus it says, "He eats (atti) that very [lotus] (alam). Having visualized this very adopted arisen maṇḍala, it should be beheld.

This has been stated by Ghaṇṭāpāda: "This very maṇḍala of the world, which arises through the sequence of the descent of the dust of the threads of karma depicted in a painting, is by its very nature established as non-dual. That which appears in the form of artificial duality is considered [to exist] for the sake of those to be trained (*vineya*). Therefore, it is not something to be accomplished by those seeking liberation, because liberation comes from seeing things as they truly are.

If such an arisen [world] exists at all times, why does the world not perceive it? Or rather, is it subverted by the force of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), or is it distorted through delusion regarding the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, which have the nature of a dream?

Therefore, one should apply oneself to vision; for while this untrustworthy perfection of the opportune moment lasts, it quickly burns away that which is to be abandoned and that which is to be adopted. Thus, he enjoins [the practitioner] to the cultivation [of this insight].

The sixth chapter [ends] in the *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the great tantra *Śrī Buddhakapāla*, composed by the scholar Abhayākaragupta. The seventh chapter, titled "The Meditation on the Arising of Heruka within the Maṇḍala," begins now. In order to explain the meditation on the Blessed One according to the Tantra of the Fruit (*phalatantra*), he first describes the external maṇḍala out of consideration for those to be trained, starting with the words "Now" (*atha*) and so forth, and "Mountain" (*giri*) and so forth;
these have their meanings according to the literal sense (*yathāruta*).
Regarding "circular" and so forth,
the sequence here is as follows:

On the mandala ground that has been prepared according to the rules—either by touching it with the hand or purified by reciting one hundred and eight times the mantra for purifying the earth—one should determine the cardinal and intermediate directions using the shadow of a gnomon and the "fish" diagram (*matsya*) according to the method taught in our own *Kālacakrāvatāra*. Then, the preceptor (*ācārya*), having assumed the form of the deity and offered the bali-offering, first faces the east. Holding with his left vajra-fist at his navel a new thread of the thickness of a barley grain, twice as long as the mandala, and exceeding it by one span (*vitasti*), which has been wound around twenty-five times representing the nature of the five Tathāgatas who are each identical to the five primordial wisdoms (*pañcajñāna*), he should, together with the disciple and others who have assumed the form of the deity, cast two threads called the "wisdom-threads" (*jñānasūtra*) into the sky, and then cast a single straight "brahma-thread" onto the ground below.
Then, for the sake of establishing the squareness of the mandala, one should lay down a second Brahma-thread facing north over the head and tail of the fish-mark;
thereafter, one should lay down the four root-threads of the mandala according to the measurement of one cubit or other units,
and then the two diagonal threads according to the prescribed rule.
Then, proceeding from the Brahma-thread toward the eastern and other directions, one should leave one thread-measure on the ground for the colored powder (rajobhūmi), omit four threads,
then omit two threads,
and finally one thread.

Thereafter, having set aside two threads, there remains only one thread for the deity-strip; thus, starting from the Brahma-thread together with the central root-thread, there are ten threads on one side, and the same sequence applies to the other sides as well.
Then, outside the root-line, one line for the colored powder-ground (*rajobhūmi*) is drawn with a measurement equal to one-fourth of a door, which itself is one-eighth of the wheel;
then, one line for the altar of the deities (*devatāvedi*) is drawn with a measurement equal to half a door;
then, one line for the jeweled band (*ratnapaṭṭikā*) is drawn with the same measurement as the colored powder-ground.
Then, one thread for the necklace (hāra), half-necklace (arddhahāra), and the fillet-band (paṭṭikā) according to the measurement of the altar (vedī);

then, according to the measurement of the colored-powder ground (rajobhūmi), one thread for the bakula-fillet (vakulāpaṭṭikā), and in the opinion of some, further, one thread for the jewel-fillet (ratnapaṭṭikā).

Then, one line for the dark band (*andhakārapaṭṭikā*) is shortened; there, the successive heads (*kramaśīrṣa*) are likewise. Then, for fear of the labor involved in erasing, four lines for the archway (*toraṇa*), which is three times the length of the door, are marked using either the shortened line or a long one.
Then, omitting two lines, one line connected to the archway remains.

[This concludes] the seventh chapter. Then, omitting three lines, one line for the positions of the bell, the wind-god (*māruta*), the banner (*patākā*), the flag (*dhvaja*), the parasol (*chatra*), the wish-granting tree (*kalpavṛkṣa*), and so forth, is established.
Again, having set aside one thread, then one thread,
and then one thread for the row of lotus petals;
therefore, the location is within the peaked pavilion situated upon the altar of the universal vajra at the center of the lotus pericarp.
Outside that altar, on the pericarp of the lotus, the universal vajra, arches, and so forth are drawn;
then one line for the vajra-fence, and then, leaving two lines, one line for the circle of light.
Some say that there is no row of lotus petals; however, a certain person from Koṅkaṇa states that there are four lines— the Vajra, Padma, Cakra, and Prabhāvalī lines—
thus making sixteen lines in total on one side, beginning with the line of the dust-particles (rajobhūmi).
In this manner, it is also [applied] to other previous sections; thus, the rule for the method of sketching the double-layered maṇḍala is found in the twenty-sixth sūtra.
Following this very direction, the method for laying out the lines for triple-layered and other maṇḍalas is to be inferred.

Likewise, by means of a single layout, the procedure for maṇḍalas comprising nine, thirteen, fifteen, nineteen, twenty-five, thirty-two, thirty-seven, up to forty thousand [deities], and so forth, is to be understood.

Regarding this, the specific details of the intermediate lines for the archways (*toraṇa*) and so forth, as well as the purification of the ground and the scattering of powdered pigments (*loparajas*), have been explained by us at length in the *Maṇḍalopāyikā*.
"Encircled by the three vajras" means it is surrounded by three rows of vajras that are blue, red, and white.

Regarding the word "instantly" (*jhaṭiti*): why? Because of the arising of the twenty-five yoginīs and the Blessed One from the syllable *HŪṂ* itself. Thus, they are said to have "issued forth" there at the time of the Blessed One’s manifestation.

From the syllable *HŪṂ*, the foundation maṇḍala—adorned with five colors—is produced; it is "of the nature of *HŪṂ*" (*hūṃkārātmikā*) in the sense that her own self (*ātmā*) has arisen from the syllable *HŪṂ*. Therefore, she is so described.

The female gatekeepers situated in the middle, second, and third enclosures are, respectively, black, fair, and dark-complexioned; however, the one standing in the center is like the central [deity] in being black.
Regarding the phrase "with Akṣobhya as his crown," this is stated because Akṣobhya, situated in the center, is the principal [deity];
for it is said in the *Pañcabuddhamudrā*: "[He is] adorned [by them]."
"All yoginīs" refers to twenty-five;

"of such form" means that just as the Bhagavān is sealed upon the head, so too are they sealed. However, he states that the Tathāgata who stands upon their heads is the leader, being distinct for each one.

Regarding the passage beginning with "paraṃ hi" and so forth: some teachers maintain that the four female gatekeepers, such as Sumālinī and the others, desire [him], or rather, they cause him to desire.
You have fallen into despondency regarding the objects of the senses because you are solely intent upon emptiness for the sake of others;
why is this so?
O Kanakavati, do you remember me, the Lord of all, who made the vow to uplift the world? Having pursued only your own self-interest, do you not recall this?
"Previously," and so forth:

remembering your previous vow as it was promised, may there be despondency (*viṣāda*)—afflicted by the suffering of *saṃsāra*—regarding that which is falsely conceptualized (*mithyā-parikalpita*). This is the commentary on the *Śrī-buddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja*, titled *Abhayapaddhati*; [it concerns] the conceit (*māna*) regarding "existence" (*bhava*) at the end of existence and "non-existence" (*abhāva*) at the end of non-existence.
If that is so, then there would be a grasping of an entity; to this he says: "phaṭṭau," and so forth.

The meaning is that through the delight of the assembly of *yoginīs*, because of the arising of great bliss which has emptiness as its single flavor, there occurs the exhaustion of the conceptual grasping at existence, non-existence, and so forth; this is as in the case of the *hetuvajradhara* [in the context of] the *pūrvajra* and other signs.
In another tantra, it is stated that the color of the Holder of the Resultant Vajra is blue, while that of the Holder of the Causal Vajra is white;
however, here [in this text], it is indeed blue,
as there is a reading stating that his color, emblem, and so forth are as previously described.
Then, it is clearly stated that even the Causal Vajradhara is blue and "upraised" (ucchrita), accompanied by Citrasenā;

for is it not the case that the Causal Vajradhara is traditionally taught to be a transformation of the moon, sun, and so forth, whose nature consists of the Mirror-like Wisdom and the other [wisdoms]? Why then is this [deity] not likewise?
Because he arises from the *hūṃ* syllable of the "Vajra-hūṃ," produced from that liquid,
is he not therefore the Vajradhara of the fruit who consists of the five gnoses?
It is not so, because these [five gnoses], being utterly pure, arise in that very form.

For instance, that knowledge which perceives the entire world as reflected like in a mirror is the knowledge of equality (*samatājñāna*), by means of which the equality of the world thus reflected is realized;
and that which is the knowledge of discernment (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), by means of which, while remaining in meditative equipoise, the mental activities of all sentient beings are discerned.

The knowledge of the performance of duties (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*) is that by which one carries out the welfare of the world as it has been thus contemplated; and the knowledge of the perfectly pure realm of phenomena (*suviśuddhadharmadhātujñāna*) is the non-duality of compassion and wisdom consisting of great bliss, liberated from the two obscurations along with their latent tendencies, which is the perfection of the realization of the *dharmadhātu*. Therefore, even the Holder of the Resultant Vajra (*phalavajradhṛk*) has these five knowledges as his essential nature; however, a beginner cultivates these knowledges through resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*).
The mind itself, being exceedingly pure like the form of the moon, is the mirror of the entire world.

At the conjunction of the moon and the sun, because all phenomena are like reflections within the mind—which consists of great bliss—no differentiation is perceived; thus, through the intention that it is the supreme means for determining the welfare of the world, it manifests as such by means of emanations to accomplish that purpose.
Once perfected through the contemplation of that object, one should practice neither too little nor too much.

Herein, according to tradition, this is the sequence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanākrama*): having performed the protection of the place, oneself, and the yoga, the mantra-practitioner—awakened by the exhortation of the four goddesses’ songs—rises in the morning and, with or without a consort, naked with hair loose, facing south for all rites, sits upon a comfortable seat in a cremation ground or another location agreeable to the mind in the vajra-posture. *Hūṃ phaṭ*, or *Oṃ āḥ hūṃ*. Having thus performed the protection of the place, self, and yoga, in a cremation ground or other place suitable to the mind, seated comfortably in the vajra-posture, whether with or without a consort, naked and with hair disheveled, he faces south in all ritual activities.

According to the divisions such as *śāntika* (pacification) and so forth, facing one's own respective direction and preceded by the service of the *samaya* substances, one should accomplish the nectar (*amṛta*) according to the sequence to be described in the seventh chapter. Having offered the *bali*, one should bring before oneself in the sky the Blessed Lord Heruka—who is seated upon the solar disc in one's own heart, firmly grasped by the vajra-fist, who reaches as far as the Akaniṣṭha heaven with the mass of rays from the syllable *Haṃ*, who is embraced by his own beloved Citrasenā, surrounded by a retinue of twenty-four vajra-dancers beginning with Sumālinī, and whose colors and other attributes will be described—facing toward oneself.

Immediately after the entry of the light rays from the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should worship with the Vajra goddesses who have emerged simultaneously from that *HŪṂ*. Therein, in the eastern direction, Vajradāḍhī causes the Lord to drink the *rajas* (pollen/seed) from a skull-cup held in her two hands in a gesture of offering a lotus;
in the northeast, Vajradūtī plays a hand-drum (*ḍamaru*) with both hands.

In the southeast, Vajraghoṇā, holding a skull-cup with the gesture of the lotus, feeds Vairocana; in the southwest, Vajriṇī likewise holds a vessel of respectful offering (arghya) filled with vajra-water and offers it;
in the south, Vajravikaṭā plays a drum (paṭaha) with both hands.
In the northwest, Vajranābhi, together with Dhṛtakapāla, offers a deer;
in the west, Vajraghorā, together with Dhṛtakapāla, devours the well-known jackal known as *luba*;
in the north, Rāgavajrī, having become one with Citrasenā, embraces her and impassions her with great passion.
Having honored and prostrated with dance, song, and so forth, one should perform the confession of sins and other practices as follows:
"I confess all my own misdeeds; I shall not commit them again.
I rejoice in all the merits of all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, noble ones, and ordinary beings."
I dedicate all my own roots of virtue toward unexcelled, perfect enlightenment.

Until I reach awakening, I take refuge in the Three Jewels: namely, the Jewel of the Buddha, the Jewel of the Dharma of the Perfection of Wisdom, and the Jewel of the Noble Saṅgha of irreversible Bodhisattvas.

Oh, may I indeed awaken to unexcelled, perfect enlightenment! May I do so by practicing that path for the sake, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings, until they reach ultimate, final Nirvāṇa and are established in the unsurpassed wisdom of a Tathāgata.

Then, embraced by the fierce *caṇḍālī* ignited by the impulsion of the wind driven from below, and pervading the entire body with rays from the *hūṃ* syllable at the heart, one should enter into the emptiness of all phenomena while bringing its meaning to mind preceded by the internal recitation: "I am of the nature of the *vajra* of the wisdom of emptiness" (*oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako’ham*).

Thereafter, through the power of attention directed toward former meditative applications, one should perform the binding of the boundary—the vajra-fence, cage, net of arrows, and canopy—by means of the radiating branches of light from the syllable *HŪṂ* situated in the center of the solar disc produced from the seed-syllable *RAṂ*, which has been transformed into a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*). Below that, upon the adamantine ground fashioned by that double-vajra, and above it, within the white triangular source of phenomena (*dharmodaya*) produced from the syllable *A*, there stands a lotus; upon its pericarp is a vajra held in a fist. O, there is nothing [else].

In the commentary on the *Śrī-Buddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja*, titled *Abhayapaddhati*, [there is] the hub of the Universal Vajra: upon a blue wind mandala, shaped like a bow with two banners and marked by the syllable *yaṃ yaṃ*, there is a red triangular fire mandala produced from the transformation of the syllable *raṃ*, emitting seven tongues of flame; at its junctions is a white water mandala, circular, marked with a vase, and containing the syllable *vaṃ*; and resting upon that is a beautiful golden earth mandala, square in shape, adorned with the syllable *laṃ*, and decorated with the four continents.

Thus, there is a peaked pavilion (kūṭāgāra) constructed from the four elements presided over by their respective seed-syllables; it is circular within, triple-layered, square on the outside, with four doors and adorned with four archways (toraṇas). It possesses four radiant altars decorated with necklaces and other ornaments, as well as celestial nymphs (apsaras);
its pillars consist of all kinds of jewels and it is embellished with small bells.
In its center, upon the pericarp of a universal eight-petaled lotus, is the corpse, whose intrinsic nature is the sphere of phenomena (dharmadhātu).

Above that, in the heart within the orb of the sun, is the lunar disc transformed from the doubled vowels, which is the cause of the thirty-two major marks and has the nature of mirror-like gnosis (*ādarśajñāna*). It is transformed from the consonants doubled with *ya, ra, la, va, ḍa, ḍha*, and is the basis for the eighty minor marks. The sun is the very form of the gnosis of equality (*samatājñāna*).

In its center is the syllable *HŪṂ*; within the hub of the five-spoked vajra produced by the recitation of *HŪṂ* is the syllable *HAṂ*, which consists of wisdom and method and has the nature of discerning gnosis (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*).

That very [deity], whose nature is the wisdom of accomplishing activities (*kṛtyānuṣṭhānajñāna*), acts for the benefit of the world in all directions through deities who emanate from the five rays of light being projected.

The Blessed One, the causal Vajradhara of Buddhakapāla—who has thus been transformed from the moon and other elements, whose nature is the wisdom of the utterly pure dharmadhātu, who possesses the luster of a freshly blossomed kadalī flower, or, according to the system of other tantras, a body with the brilliance of jasmine-white, or who has arms and so forth like the resultant Vajradhara to be described later, and who is embraced by the red Citrasenā—is to be meditated upon as the very cause for the manifestation of the Blessed One from the syllable *HŪṂ*, surrounded by the twenty-four goddesses beginning with Sumālinī who have already been manifested.
Some of our teachers say that even at this point in the procedure, the Blessed One drinks the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) contained in the skull-cup offered by the twenty-four goddesses.

Following that, having visualized *oṃ āḥ hūṃ svāhā* respectively upon Citrasenā’s head, throat, heart, secret place, and thighs, her body is pervaded by those [syllables] as they flash forth from one another; and within the center of the red lotus born from the syllable *hrīḥ*, there is the red syllable *āḥ*.

Having visualized the Bhagavān-vajra, born from the black syllable *HŪṂ*, its tip empowered by the white syllable *OṂ*, the twenty-four goddesses—indistinguishable from Citrasenā—desire the Bhagavān through the union of such a vajra and lotus.

And the Bhagavān, beginning the act of passion with the mantra *OṂ SARVATATHĀGATĀNURĀGAṆAVAJRASVABHĀVĀTMAKO ’HAM* ("I am the self-nature of the passion-vajra of all Tathāgatas"), melts together with the Bhagavatī through great passion. This, situated upon the sun, is the first meditative absorption (*samādhi*) called the "Initial Yoga."
Therein, due to their fluidity and in consideration of their previous specific vows, the four goddesses manifest as vibrations;
not seeing the Lord in the mandala, they, longing for him, awaken the Master with songs, saying: "O Bho Dā! O Bho Sā! [This is] the seventh chapter.

In this regard, Sumālinī, whose nature is great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*), having invited the world to her task with constant perseverance, says: "If you do not remember how things were, arise; all sorrows shall vanish. Thus [ends] these two songs.
O Kāpālinī, whose nature is great compassion, even though you have made me your own, do not cause me pain; O heart, I entreat you.

"Everyone has fallen into the fear of existence; arise for the sake of the yoginī! O you who are by nature terrifying and greatly joyful, just as you previously understood, accomplish that task! Therefore, having honored everyone, abandon the pride of the mind. With these words, [the yoginī] is difficult to conquer and characterized by indifference. "Do not practice deceit or pride; there is a state of voidness in the maternal uncle's lineage. O yoginī, desire the assembly; let your [attachment] fall away, or else be mindful! With these words, following such an exhortation, the Blessed Lord Heruka—born from the *hūṃ* produced from that very essence—is manifested. He is dark blue in color, with one face and four arms; with his two right hands he holds a *ḍamaru* drum and a flaying knife (*kartṛ*), and with his left hands a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and a skull-cup (*kapāla*).

He reclines upon the breast of the maiden who dwells within the lotus of the universe; he wears a half-moon disc fixed upon his head; he performs the dance of the nine dramatic sentiments, beginning with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*); he possesses a row of fifty-one human heads serving as a support for his dance;

he has made a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) from wet intestines; on his back he wears a dripping tiger skin, while in front he is naked; he holds a discus, wears earrings, a necklace, armlets, a girdle, and anklets resounding with a jingling *ghūghūra* sound; he is crowned by the five Buddhas; [and] at his neck...
