The *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the *Śrī Buddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja*: Upon a mass of matted hair marked by the half-moon of the Universal Vajra (*viśvakuliśa*), he wears a garland of five skulls bound around the crown of his forehead; adorned with the ashes of funeral pyres, he possesses a body that is both artificially wrathful and exceedingly fierce. His three eyes blaze with the radiance of a rising orb of sunbeams. He has vanquished and pulverized the hosts of arrogant Māras with the roar of the syllable *HŪṂ*.
With supreme love and great compassion, he rescues embodied beings submerged in the cavern of the ocean of *saṃsāra*. He is to be meditated upon by the yogi who has fixed his breath within.

And the beloved of this Lord, Citrasenā, was born together with the Blessed One from the syllable *Hūṃ*; she is naked, adorned with rays of light, having cast off her garland of human heads; her loose, tawny, upward-flaming hair is bound by skulls possessing the luster of *bandhūka* flowers; her body possesses waves of playful beauty; she has slightly fierce fangs, one face, and three eyes; she playfully embraces the neck of her Lord; and with her left hand, she causes the Lord to drink from a stream of nectar flowing from the opening of a skull-cup held in her lap, which emerged from her own lotus-like mouth. With her right arm raised above him in the gesture of striking down the hosts of obstacles on the path to liberation for those dwelling in the three worlds, she flows with semen through the amorous arts of the four joys—such as the application of cooling nectar and other delights.
Delightfully pleasing the heart of her husband with intense devotion,
at the time of the birth of this couple, the Vajra-nymphs such as Sumālinī and others were born;
among them, Sumālinī was born from the eastern petal of the Lord's seat.
In the north is Kāpālinī, in the west Bhīmā, and in the south Durjayā;
in the intermediate petals starting from the northeast, there are skull-cups filled with semen, blood, the five nectars, and the five lamps, arranged in a clockwise direction.
This first enclosure is an eight-petalled lotus encircled by a garland of blue vajras;
then the second enclosure is an eight-petalled lotus situated upon an eight-spoked red wheel, encircled on all sides externally by a garland of fresh, vermilion-red thunderbolts;
on its eastern spoke is Śubhamekhalā.
Rūpiṇī is in the north,
Vijayā in the west, and Kāriṇī in the south.
Kālinī is in the northeast,
Mahodadhi in the southeast, and Kāriṇī in the southwest.
In the northwest is Māriṇī;
then, the third enclosure consists of eight white lotuses situated upon a white eight-spoked wheel, encircled by a garland of white vajras; in its eastern petal is Tāriṇī.
In the north is Bhīmadarśanā, in the west Sudarśanā,
and in the south Ajayā.
In the northeast is Śubhā, in the southeast is Ostārakī, and in the southwest is Kālarātrī.
In the northwest is Mahāyaśā;
then at the eastern gate is Padmasundarī,
and in the north is Vasundharā on a lotus.
On the western lotus is Subhagā, and on the southern lotus is Priyadarśanā;

all of these have their left hands—like tender sprouts—engaged in grasping a skull-cup and a curved knife, with their lips quivering in the state of being a consort and their single faces showing slightly protruding teeth. They are naked, devoid of ornaments, and lack garlands of severed heads; they are the Bone-Eaters, the Vajra-Tārīs, with masses of loose hair tawny and blazing upward. This is the seventh chapter.

From excessive passion, they cause semen to flow; dancing with one leg in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), they resemble the beautiful orb of the sun amidst fresh, blossoming *mandāra* flowers.

As for the four door-keepers: all of them stand in the *pratyālīḍha* stance, are clothed in tiger skins, possess blazing radiance, have three eyes, and stream streams of blood from their mouths. They are an ocean of aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), and their bodies are white in color like freshly split slabs of sapphire. Alternatively, the four beginning with Sumālinī are black, while those in the second enclosure are fair-complexioned.
The four female deities of the doors situated on the third enclosure are dark-complexioned;
others, however, our teachers [maintain], are Sumālinī, who is white,
and Kāpālinī, who is yellow.
Bhīmā, Śubhrā, Durjayā, Kṛṣṇā, Dvitīyapuṭinī, and Raktā.
Those situated in the third enclosure are white:
Sundarī is white and Vasundharā is yellow.
They say that [the goddesses] Subhagā, Pītā, Priyadarśanā, and Kṛṣṇā are to be meditated upon according to one's preference, as they are described in detail in the Tantras.
Since both sides are taught in the *Laghutantra*,
from there [the seed-syllables] are placed: OṂ at the heart of the Blessed One and HOṂ on the forehead.
HAIṂ at the throat;
HAIṂ at the crest-lock; HOṂ at the two shoulders.
Hauṃ at the two eyes, Haṃ at the secret place, and Haḥ throughout the entire body.
Thus is the armor.
Following that, in the heart is Kṛṣṇa with HŪṂ at the center of the vajra; in the throat is Raktā with ĀḤ at the center of the transformed lotus.

Having bestowed the empowerment of mind, speech, and body by means of the syllable *oṃ* in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*) and the syllable *oṃ* in the navel wheel (*jātacakre*), one draws in the wisdom circle (*jñānacakra*) with rays of light from the syllable *hūṃ* situated upon a vajra at the heart of a sun disk. Having dispelled obstacles with the syllable *hūṃ* and offered the water of honor (*arghya*), one should—by means of the four female gatekeepers in their respective order, using *jaḥ*, *hūṃ*, *vaṃ*, and *hoḥ*—draw them in, cause them to enter, bind them, and subjugate them. Then, reciting with pride: *oṃ buddhakāpālinī āḥ khaṃ kroṃ ṅ khūṃ āṃ āṃ āṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ*, one should visualize the pledge mandala (*samayamaṇḍala*) as having become a single, unified mass with that [wisdom mandala].

Then, at the time of bathing the seed-syllable of the Dharma-wheel (*dharmacakra*) with the nectar situated in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*), which has gradually melted through the blazing Caṇḍālī at the navel, the eight *nāḍīs* that constitute the nature of the Dharma-wheel—being composed of great bliss—manifest as the Ḍākinīs of the Wild Jackal (*kroṣṭu*) during the time of worship. These twelve Cāriṇīs are the ground for the unsurpassed beauty and grace of various garments and ornaments; they hold in their bud-like hands vases filled with the bodhicitta of mango blossoms; they are peaceful, smiling, radiant, and quivering. Then, from the moon, the four syllables—*nāsti*, *bho rakta*, *bho hūṃ*, and *bho aṃ aṃ aḥ*—issue forth. This concludes the commentary on the Great King of Tantras, the *Śrī Buddhakapāla*, titled the *Abhayapaddhati*.

At that very moment, may those compassionate ones, together with the Tathāgatas and goddesses of the ten directions drawn by the rays of light from my heart-seed syllable, sprinkle me; bowing down again and again with palms joined, I entreat them:

"May all the Yoginīs consecrate me; may they empower this crown; may they come! HŪṂ SVĀHĀ! With these words, they—filled with supreme compassion, holding pure white full vases in their hands, and accompanied by parasols, banners, flags, garments, music, and all other offerings—consecrate one with the outer, secret, wisdom, and fourth initiations while crying out "Victory! Victory! and so forth.
At the time of consecration, within the maṇḍala of the syllable *jyau*, the sound of a drum resounds from the sky, followed by a rain of sandalwood, saffron, flowers, and other offerings; thereafter,
those [deities] dissolve into their respective channels (*nāḍī*), and subsequently,
the Blessed One and the goddesses are to be sealed by the lords of their own respective families.

In that regard, because of the statement, "The Blessed One Vajrasattva is adorned by the five Buddhas," [the deities are assigned as follows]: Citrasenā, Mahāvairocanī, Sumālinī, and so forth—those situated in the second enclosure—are with Akṣobhya and the other [Buddhas]; those situated in the third enclosure are with Ratnasambhava; and [the central deity] is with Vairocana.
One should seal the female gatekeepers with Amoghasiddhi;
then, having emerged from those eight ṭāḍīs, the eight yoginīs worship the Lord as before by means of [the mantra] that has Vajrasattva as its other name.

"O Vajrakanyā, you whose form has gradually transformed into the bliss of abundant nectar through the union of the lotus and the vajra, performing your dance for the sake of the welfare of sentient beings—perceive this play! O you who have become the ground of delusion and pride, bowing before you, who bestows immeasurable joy upon the world, is our refuge. Having thus praised her, one should taste the nectar, impelled by the sounds of the pleasure of the Blessed Lord and the Blessed Lady.
When the five Tathāgatas have arrived and entered through the door of Vairocana, they melt and fall into the interior of the lotus;
then, one should personally partake of the inner nectar of the five wisdoms with the tip of the tongue moving gracefully, and satisfy the deities of the maṇḍala.

As for the outer [offering], there is a wind mandala, blue in color, with two fluttering banners, born from the syllable *ya~* and containing the syllable *ya~*; within that is a fire mandala, red and possessing seven flames, born from the transformation of the syllable *ra~* and containing the syllable *ra~*.

Above that, resting upon three skulls produced from the three syllables, is a lotus born from the syllable *Āḥ*. [One recites: "O *Abhiṣiñcantu*, O *Maṅgala*, O *Mukuṭa*, O *Devī*, O *Saptama*. Within that vessel are the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) and the five meats (*pañcamāṃsa*), transformed from the syllables *Vi-ra-śu-ma-mu-go-ku-da-ha-na* together with the half-moon and the *anusvāra*, accompanied by *Oṃ Hūṃ Khaṃ Svāḥ Hūṃ*. Then, as the liquid substance within the skull is heated by the fire fanned by the wind, through contact with the purified vapors, it melts and enters the blue thunderbolt (*vajra*) containing the syllable *Hūṃ* situated one span (*vitasti*) above in the intermediate space. Upon its complete transformation into a single flavor, the orb of the moon presided over by the syllable *Jauṃ* is located one span above; and by the rays of light from the syllable *Oṃ*, the Tathāgatas and others residing in the ten directions enter along with the nectar of the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta-amṛta*) and the special powers of jewels, mantras, and medicinal herbs. Having consecrated all of this as nectar—cool like a mass of snow and possessing the nature of the three triads—one should satisfy oneself, the deities of the mandala, and the tongue which is a single-pointed vajra marked by the white *Hūṃ* and its rays. This is the second meditative absorption (*samādhi*) named the King of Mandalas (*maṇḍalarāja*).

Then, impelled by the Blessed One, all the Ḍākinīs and the Blessed One, having accomplished the welfare of sentient beings through the radiations of clouds of bodies and having generated the attainment of the state of the Great Vajra, should withdraw them from the clouds of their own bodies back into the root body. This is the third meditative stabilization called "The Supreme King of Rituals.
Following that, one should manifest the internal arisen maṇḍala;
therein, at Pullīramalaya in the head, is Sumālinī.
Kāpālinī is at Jālandhara in the crest-lock;
Bhīmā is at Uḍḍiyāṇa in the right ear;
Durjayā is at Arbuda on the back of the head.
The seat is the stage of Pramuditā;
Sundarī is at the left ear in Godāvarī;
Vasundharī is at the center of the eyebrows in Rāmeśvarī.
Devīkoṭya is at the two eyes; Subhagā is at the two shoulders of Mālava; Priyadarśanā is at the secondary seat (upapīṭha); Vimalā is the ground.
These eight are the Khecarīs in the mind-wheel:
Śubhamekhalā is in the two armpits at Kāmarūpa,
and Rūpiṇī is in the two breasts at Uḍra.
The field is Prabhākarī; in Triśakti it is at the navel, Vijayā;
in Kośala it is at the tip of the nose, Kāriṇī.
The subsidiary field (upakṣetra) is the Arciṣmatī stage;
Vijayī is at the navel in Triśaknu, and Kāriṇī is at the tip of the nose in Kauśala.
The subsidiary field (upakṣetra) is the Arciṣmatī stage;
Kaliṅgamukha is Kālinī;
Lampāka is the Great Ocean at the throat; and the place of pilgrimage (chandoha) is the Sudurjayā stage.
Kāriṇī is in Kāñcī, Māriṇī is in the heart, and Abhimukhī is on the ground at Himālaya; this is the secondary meter (upachandoha).
In the wheel of speech is Bhūcaryā;
in Pretapurī, at the linga, is Tāriṇī;
and in the house-deity, at the anus, is Bhīmadarśanā.
Melāpaka is the stage Dūraṅgamā;
Saurāṣṭra is on the two thighs; Sudarśanā is on the shanks in Suvarṇadvīpa; Ajayā is on the calves.
The mountain is the place of assembly; the earth is the immovable one;
the auspicious pill is desired in the city;
in the ocean, [it is found] on the surface of the feet.
Stārakī is at the feet;
Sādhumatī is the ground;
Kālarātrī is at the two big toes.
In Kulatā, at the knees: O Jihvā! O Mahāvajradhara! O Mahāyaśas!
Upaśmaśāna is the Dharmameghā bhūmi;
they are the Pātālavāsinyas in the body wheel.
The fourfold set beginning with bodhicitta resides in the fourfold set of wheels beginning with Mahāsukha;
it is the location of the two pericarp centers of the Blessed One and Citrasenā.
Here, she embraces him through radiance.
In accordance with the instruction, in accordance with reality, and in accordance with liberation, through the meditative cultivation of the various divisions of Caṇḍālī,
all that— from the perspective of ultimate truth—
should be visualized as having the very nature of Citrasenā-Buddhakapāla, whose essential form is inseparable from emptiness, great bliss, and compassion, and who is the world itself.

Furthermore, if the yogin wishes to stabilize the mind for the swift accomplishment of all siddhis, then, in brief, having visualized the three samādhis, he should place a blue *āḥ* at the opening of the knot above the sixty-four-petaled lotus of the *nirmāṇacakra*, which faces upward; a blue *hūṃ* at the downward-facing eight-spoked *dharmacakra*;
a red *oṃ* at the upward-facing sixteen-spoked *saṃbhogacakra*;
and a white *haṃ* at the downward-facing thirty-two-spoked *mahāsukhacakra*.

One should meditate on the Hero (vīra), who is of the nature of Caṇḍī impelled by the wind and fire residing in the secret wheel (*guhyacakra*), as the letter *aṃ*—melted by the rays blazing from the letter *aṃ* and inseparable from the three syllables beginning with *hūṃ*. Having become a drop consisting of innate bliss (*sahajānanda*), one should resolve upon the maturation of that meditation. From that very [drop], one should visualize a subtle line of light rays remaining like a single blazing flame.
By its power, the Hero and that line of light rays, drenched by a flood of flowing nectar, become cooled.
Then, having restrained the mind upon the hero, one should observe it for as long as it takes to perceive through signs the attainment of stability of the mind.
Once stability has been perceived, one should contemplate the clear light of that line of rays illuminating the entire universe, and see everything like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand;
thus one should swiftly accomplish all meditative absorptions—this is the *binduyoga*.
One should meditate upon the various forms of Caṇḍālī according to the instruction and according to one's inclination.
It is said that for one who has recited the vidyā-mantra, success is attained;
therefore, this root mantra is to be recited when one becomes weary from meditation.
Oṃ hrīḥ buddha hūṃ kāpālini āḥ! This is the sequence for recitation:
when the breath from the nostrils enters the drop (bindu) located between the navel and the [upper] region, [one recites] Oṃ.
HĪḤ when it emerges from the nostrils;
HŪṂ when it abides in the bliss of the Buddha-bindu; Kāpālinī at its setting.
At the arising of the drop, "Āḥ.
Thus, from the recitation of the six limbs, the vajra-recitation and the subtle yoga are to be understood in this very manner.
Oṃ buddhakāpālinī āḥ hrīḥ haiṃ hūṃ phaṭ is the heart mantra.
Oṃ! O Buddhakāpālinī, you who abide in the pair of lotus navels—Bhoḥ!
[The word] "ṣaḍa" does not exist—Bhoḥ! The seventh chapter: Vajriṇī, hau! O invincible one, O difficult to perceive! Hūṃ phaṭ! This is the upahr̥daya-mantra.
Having recited one of these mantras according to his preference at the time of rising, he should offer the *sārvabhautika* bali with this mantra:

Oṃ buddhakāpālavajre citteṣu catre alaṃbale prīṇaya sarvabhūtān māraya sarvamārān kīlaya sarvaduṣṭānuccāṭaya sarvavighnān vitrāpaya bho bhagavati yakṣarākṣasapiśācān śoṣaya tāḍaya saptapātālagatān | sara sara prasara prasara hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ ||

Having offered [the offering] with this mantra, and having dedicated all this merit toward unexcelled perfect enlightenment and the attainment of one's desired goal, one should perform the worship as before. Then, one should internalize the twenty-four mandalas into the channels located at the twenty-four sites, such as the *pīṭhas*, within one's own body, according to the oral instructions. [The skull-cup of bodhicitta is placed] in the wheel of great bliss (*mahāsukhacakra*).
One should visualize a skull-cup of *rajas* for the emanation,

a skull-cup of the five nectars in the heart, and a skull-cup of the five lamps in the *Aṅkula*; having thus internalized these, one should dwell as one pleases, with a conviction that oneself and the entire limitless triple world are of the nature of illusory appearance (*māyāmayam*), consisting of great bliss whose single flavor is emptiness, and whose form is the Blessed Lord embraced by the Blessed Lady.

At midday, evening, and midnight, during the junctions of the day, one should perform the entire sequence beginning with the armor (*kavaca*) by means of the circle of the entire harem, which has been expanded through the easy path of the *sandhyā*.

At the time of sleep, however, as before, one should resolve that oneself consists of the innate bliss (*sahajānanda*) whose nature is emptiness liquefied, and that sleep likewise has that same nature; then one should sleep.
When the desire to arise occurs, having suddenly awakened due to the exhortation of the four goddesses as previously described, one should perceive everything exactly as it was, without omission.

In this manner, one should bathe daily according to the ritual of consecration until the signs of accomplishment are obtained; likewise, one should consume all food according to the ritual for tasting nectar (*amṛta*).

Furthermore, when this very Blessed One is meditated upon as devoid of conceptual wisdom (*niṣprajña*), then there is the textual passage beginning with "the Causal Vajradhara" and ending with "the Blessed Lord Heruka.
And regarding this Lord, the passage beginning with "his beloved consort" and ending with "because it is stated in the *Laghutantra*" [is to be applied].
The section beginning with "by the four" and ending with "having brought under control"; the section beginning with "that" and ending with "should seal";
the section beginning with "the Blessed Lady" and ending with "should please";
and the section beginning with "thereafter, internally" and ending with "by means of the meditation on the distinctions."
From "Citrasenā" up to "having embraced by the twenty-four [goddesses]" and so forth;
"become liquefied as before" means that,
as previously stated, with the exception of the exhortation by the four goddesses, everything else that was said, is to be said, and is to be known.
However, O Lord, there is no "HŪṂ" for this Blessed One in the east or north;
[it is located] in the *nirmāṇacakra*, O Lord,
and in the throat, O Lord.
In the commentary on the *Śrī Buddhakāpāla-mahātantrarāja* titled *Abhayapaddhati*, [the goddesses] are situated respectively upon the petals of the inner speech-lotus:

Citrasenā, Kāminī, Pātālavāsinī, and Saubhadrā. Born from the seed-syllables OṂ HŪṂ KHAṂ SVAḤ, they are blue in color, stand in the pratyālīḍha posture, and wear tiger-skin garments. With their two right hands they hold a curved knife (*kartti*) and a skull-cup (*kapāla*); with their two left hands they carry a khaṭvāṅga staff and a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*).

In the petals of the northeast, southeast, southwest, and northwest, there are, in due order, Śauṇḍinī, Bhūtinī, Caturbhujā, and Khecarī, transformed from the syllables *hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ*. They are yellow in color, their bodies radiating yellow rays of light, and they stand in the *ālīḍha* posture. With their two right hands they hold a flaying knife (*kartī*) and a hand-drum (*ḍamaruka*), and with their two left arms they carry a skull-topped staff (*khaṭvāṅga*) and a lotus vessel (*padmabhājana*) adorned with flower clusters. These eight [deities] are filled with the overflowing of the most exquisite sentiments (*rasa*), such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).

They should be visualized as dancing within circles of newly risen suns; their lotus-faces are slightly terrifying with bared fangs, and their tawny hair stands erect and blazing. They wear garlands of five skulls, and are adorned with earrings, necklaces, bracelets, girdles, armlets, and anklets made of human bone that jingle. A row of fifty fresh human heads hangs from their throats. Their radiance expands like the fire at the end of an aeon, swallowing the circle of the gods. Utterly terrible with loud, boisterous laughter, they have one face from which blood flows, three eyes, and four arms; they terrify the serpents excessively and gaze directly at the Lord.
In this context, because of the statement that "the Blessed One Vajrasattva is adorned with a crown of the five Buddhas," he should be marked by Akṣobhya and the other four Buddhas.
As for Citrasena and the others, they are marked respectively by Akṣobhya, Vairocana, Ratnasaṃbhava, and Amitābha; and the same applies to Śauṇḍinī and the others.
Furthermore, the internal satisfaction through nectar occurs precisely through the meditation on the various manifestations of Caṇḍālī.

Thus, the Blessed Lord Heruka, encircled by the eight goddesses who sport with the vajras, is to be meditated upon in the applications of the *cāra* for invisibility and in the applications of the *gāruḍa*.
However, in the ritual for bathing a barren woman, he is accompanied by a consort (*saprajña*).
Furthermore, in the accomplishment of a *vidyādhara*, the Blessed Lord and the goddesses of the cardinal directions are white, while the goddesses of the intermediate directions are red.
Regarding the ritual bathing for a barren woman or one whose children have died, this Blessed One is endowed with wisdom;
however, when he is without wisdom, the text is abandoned, and it should be adopted according to what is appropriate.
Furthermore, one should visualize this entire gabled palace as being surrounded by eight cremation grounds.
To its east is the cremation ground named Caṇḍogra, also known by the name Sādhakānugraha; there is a śirīṣa tree or a pāṭali tree;
the guardians of the direction are the highly powerful Indra and Upendra, who have the faces of an elephant and a buffalo respectively;
and the nāga is Śuklavāsuki.
The cloud named Garjita;

in the southeast, the cremation ground called Aṭṭahāsa, also known as the Great Dissolution (Mahāpralaya); the Karañja or Udumbara tree; the goat-faced or dog-faced [deity]; the fire of great supernatural power (maharddhika); the white Mahāpadma lotus; and the Ghanodadhi cloud.
In the south, [the deity] stands in the ālīḍha posture, adorned with eight nāgas. O Bhagavatī!

O Agnideva! The seventh chapter: the Kaṅkeli, the Bhīṣaṇa, the cremation ground also known as Ghorāndhakāra, the Āmra, or the Śirīṣa; Mahiṣamukha or Vyāghravadana; the highly powerful Yama; the Śubhrapadma, the Āvarta, and the Megha.

In the southwest is the *Kilakilānāda* cremation ground, also known by the name *Mahāmelāpakayogabahula*; there stands either a *parkaṭī* or a *vaṭa* tree, and the great-iddhi *rākṣasa* Śavāsya or Gṛdhravaktra; the blue *ananta* cloud is the *prapūraṇa*. In the west is the *Jvalākula* cremation ground, also known as *Krodhānala*; there stands either a *kaṅkola* or a mango tree, and the great-iddhi Varuṇa with a makara face or an owl face; the green *karkoṭaka* cloud is the *ghora*.

In the northwest is the Ghorāndhakāra cremation ground; its tree is the Aśvattha, also known as Siṃhanāda or Mahāphūtkāra, or else the Arjuna; its deity is Mṛgamukha or Śūkarāsya, who possesses great supernatural power (maharddhika); its Yakṣa is Karburakulika, its Rākṣasa is Varṣaṇa, and its Cloud is Megha. In the north is the Gaṅgara cremation ground; its tree is the Aśvattha, also known as Advaitakara, or else the Kaṅkalli; its deity has a human face or a cat’s face and possesses great supernatural power; its Yakṣa and Vināyaka are Kubera and [Vināyaka]; its Nāga is Raktatakṣaka; its Fire is Ghūrṇita, which is red and filled with flames from the mass of his eyebrows, matted locks, and beard; he is corpulent, seated upon a goat, and holds the gestures of fearlessness (abhaya), a rosary (akṣamālā), a water-pot (kamaṇḍalu), and a staff (daṇḍa).
Kāla stands in the pratyālīḍha posture; Kāla is seated upon a buffalo, his hair blazing upward, enraged, and holding a staff and a threatening gesture in his hands.
Likewise, Śvāsana, naked, adorned with human bones,
with a face made terrifying by fangs, holds a curved knife and a skull-cup.

In the commentary on the *Śrībuddhakāpāla-mahātantrarāja*, titled *Abhayapaddhati*, Varuṇa is in Capricorn; he is white with seven hoods, holds a noose, and is mounted upon a yellow deer. Vāyu is green, wears a garment of wind, and is in Aries.
In the case of a human, he is yellow and stout; in the case of a yakṣa, he is a mongoose holding a citron.
When he is white, he has the face of an elephant and holds a root, a staff, and sweetmeats, appearing as a mouse.
Īśāna is white, mounted upon a bull, bearing matted locks and a mass of bones; his hands are occupied with a skull-topped staff marked by a trident and a ḍamaru drum.
There are eight hooded serpents with human faces who are well-adorned and remain unspecified; these sixteen, beginning with Śakra, have their beloveds embraced by their left sides.
They should be known as being near the trees, with hands in various graceful poses: Rākṣasa, Yama, and Agni in the sun; and others, radiant like the moon, in the moon.

Having abandoned their abodes, these eight of great supernatural power—Śakra, Yama, the Rākṣasas, and Īśa, who wears a jeweled crown and possesses a head radiant with gems—displayed the left half of their former bodies. With skull-bowls held aloft in their [left] hands, they are intent on the gesture of seizing [the offerings] with their other [right] hands, which hold the *bali* offerings. The *dharmamudrā* consists of speech that reveals the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*), appearing in various forms through the empowerment of the *dharmakāya* and *saṃbhogakāya*.
The *karmamudrā* is the *nirmāṇakāya*, because it accomplishes activities through various emanations by way of performing deeds (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna*).

In the generation stage (*utpattikrama*), however, the external wisdom (*prajñā*) herself, who has been meditated upon in the form of the chosen deity, is the action-seal (*karmamudrā*); she is also known by the alternative name "intrinsic consort" (*svābhāṅganā*).
Furthermore, that which is meditated upon within the body as the syllable *hūṃ* and so forth is the dharma-seal (*dharmamudrā*).

The *samayamudrā*, however, is the maṇḍala-circle produced from the seed-syllables (*bīja*) and so forth; thus, the deities are those who perform the functions of radiating and reabsorbing [light]. The *mahāmudrā* is indicated as the very form of the central deity (*nāyakadevatā*), even though it is a symbol (*cihna*).
In order to explain that internal wisdom (*prajñā*) itself takes the form of the sense-faculties, the afflictions, and the objects, he says "Now," and so forth.
"Taste" (*rasa*) refers to the tongue (*rasanā*).
"Manam" (the mind) here refers to the body-faculty as characterized by the mental faculty;

furthermore, based on the words to be spoken later, such as "How could the sister be form? and so forth, it should be understood that the objects of the eyes and other senses—form and the rest—are also of the nature of the sister and so on.
As for "by which": because that form is the cause of delusion (*moha*), it is "delusion"; and through its connection with form, hatred and the like are also included.
Passion is also passion,
pride is also pride,
and envy is also envy.
The meaning is that objects such as form (rūpa) are designated as "delusion" and so forth because they generate delusion and the like, but not in reality.
Regarding the phrase "of the mind" (cittasya), these specific states—such as the eye, delusion, and form—are merely particular conditions of the mind itself;
and the mind is indeed impure, being the very stain of delusion and the rest.
Therefore, the intention is that the eyes and so forth are also impure;
how then is it said that their remainder is the nature of wisdom (prajñā) such as the "sister" and so on?
To this he says: "Therefore... (tasmāt).

Those who are deluded are indeed pure; their wisdom is the very purity of the mind, and thus their purity is the purification of the mind. To the question "Who [should purify the mind]?", he says: "The one of great wisdom. Great wisdom is the Mahāmudrā;
the practitioner of that [wisdom] is the one who purifies everything through its very nature by washing away all impurities.
Therefore, it is said: "one whose mind is intensely united.
This means one who has transcended the duality of existence and non-existence, and whose singular essence is the non-duality of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*).
If one does not meditate in this way, then the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā will not occur. This concludes the *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the great king of tantras, the *Śrī-Buddhakapāla*.

However, when through diligent and uninterrupted cultivation there arises purity consisting of self-cognized great bliss (*svasaṃviditamahāsukha*), then— according to the words of the Blessed One, "One who desires accomplishment should not remain for even a moment with a mind directed elsewhere"— in this very human birth, upon the fulfillment of the accumulations of merit and wisdom (*puṇyajñānasaṃbhāra*) consisting of diligent and uninterrupted cultivation, [accomplishment is attained] in a single [lifetime].

In the absence of such deficiencies in one's state of being, one obtains in another existence births of indefinite number that are free from the eight inopportune conditions (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*) and conducive to practice;

through that practice, one becomes purified. However, in the system of the *Pāramitās*, it is stated that purification occurs over three incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*) due to the accumulation of merit consisting of ritual action and the absence of specific skillful means (*upāya-viśeṣa*); thus, there is no contradiction.
But [one might object]: "In this [system], nothing to be cultivated (*bhāvya*) has been taught, since the instruction consists merely in the sealing (*mudraṇa*) of those forms already arisen."
And because it is indicated for yogins precisely by means of that [non-existence], it is true;

for in reality, since all phenomena (*dharma*) are primordially peaceful, the conceptualization of the object of cultivation, the subject who cultivates, and the act of cultivation is untenable. Thus, he shows this with the words "non-existence" and so forth:

"Non-existence" refers to the negation of the superimposition of existence and non-existence regarding non-arising in the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). How indeed could there be existence, cultivation, or the like? Because they are primordially pure.

One might object: "Is it not the case that non-arising (*anutpāda*) exists as a reality (*tattva*) to be cultivated? To this he replies: "What kind of non-existence is it? Non-arising does not exist [as a substantial entity];
however, because it is conducive to the realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is called the "ultimate reality" (*paramārtha-tattva*).
Even that non-existence which consists of conventional truth is not something to be cultivated, because it is itself non-existent;
for liberation occurs merely through the vision of the non-duality of the two truths.

The point is that for those who have attained the stage of the "yoked pair" (yuganaddha), there is no longer any dogmatic adherence (*abhiniveśa*) to the notions of "that which is to be cultivated," "the cultivator," or "the act of cultivation."
This has been stated in the *Śrīsamāja*:
"In the absence [of an object], there is no cultivation; cultivation is not truly cultivation. Thus, being (*bhāva*) would not be being, and cultivation is not perceived.
For this very reason, he concludes: "How could there be cultivation? Therefore, it is not perceived"—this is the sense.
In that case, is there a total cessation of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) in the stage of the arisen (*utpannakrama*)? It is not a cessation; rather, what kind of cultivation will be described?

Desiring to refute attachment to form and so forth by first refuting attachment to the objects of cultivation and so forth from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), he says, in the thirteenth chapter, "Sister," and so on.

How so? Because one whose mind is impure will perceive form—distinguished by differences such as white and so forth—which, when conjoined with the sense faculty, is connected [to it] through a relationship of mutual assistance;

however, one whose mind is pure does not [so perceive], because in ultimate reality the sense faculties, their objects, and the cognitions thereof are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Thus it shall be explained further below.
"It is threefold" means according to the distinction between the agreeable, the disagreeable, and the neutral;
"of one endowed with such yoga" refers to this.
One who is engaged in the yoga of Mahāmudrā [perceives that] it is smelled, thus [there is] the nose and the odor;
"not being seen" means not being perceived or known.

For this very reason, passion, aversion, and so forth do not arise from odors and the like in the form of taste; thus, the nature of taste does not exist because of the absence of both the tongue and flavor. By means of the mind—indicated here by the word *manas*—and the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), one experiences pleasure born of the object of touch; by way of implication (*upalakṣaṇāt*), one also experiences pain and equanimity.

The connection is as follows: "What is that mental faculty like which experiences mental pleasure— and by way of illustration, pain, joy, dejection, and equanimity— and what is that [experience] like?"

Now, how is it that the five objects—form and so forth—their five corresponding faculties, such as the eye, and their five cognitions are established as being of the nature of the five wisdoms? Regarding the sixth object, faculty, and cognition, it is said:
the mental faculty (*manaindriya*) does not exist separately like the eye and other faculties;
rather, the very consciousness that has just passed away is called the mental faculty because it exercises sovereignty over the arising of the subsequent specific cognition.
Its distinction consists of the mind and mental factors, as well as the mental consciousness whose object is that [mind].

Among these, the mind and the sense-faculties, along with their objects, are non-conceptual; they possess the nature of the five sensory cognitions, and the mental factors are not other than the minds themselves.
Thus it has been said: "Mental factors are not other than the mind.
However, the two types of conceptualization are of the nature of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Furthermore, mental consciousness consists of [the functions of] cutting off, reconnecting, detachment, falling away, death, and birth.

According to the principle that it is intended as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) alone, and because of its predominance, it is the "experiencer"; thus, the form of wisdom (*prajñārūpa*) is established as neither an instrument nor an object of experience.
Furthermore, the state of being unsurpassed wisdom has already been established; this indeed exists within the mental consciousness, which is what was referred to as "mind" (*manas*).
Therefore, here, for the purpose of proceeding with the investigation of the entire collection of entities,
eighteen elements (dhātus) have been stated by this continuous exposition; these same [elements], when condensed, constitute the twelve bases (āyatanas).
In extremely brief summary, the five aggregates and the triple world are right there; and that is merely mind.
As it is said in the *Laṅkāvatāra*: "O sons of the Victorious One, 'merely mind' refers to the triple world."

And it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna in the *Bodhicittavivaraṇa*: "The teaching of the aggregates, elements, and so forth— that too has been demolished by the illustrious ones through the establishment of 'mind-only'. And that mind is conventional; as it is stated in that very same work: "The Sage’s teaching that 'all this is mind-only' is for the sake of removing the fear of the ignorant; it is not [the truth] in reality."
How is the mind unreal? He says:
because of the investigation of both, that is, because of the examination of the nature of existence and non-existence.
In that case, one might say that the investigating mind exists ultimately; to this he says:
"Investigation.
That which investigates is "investigation"—namely, the investigating consciousness. When both [subject and object] are investigated, that [investigating consciousness] does not exist.

As it was said by the noble Śāntidevapāda: "When that which is to be investigated has been thus investigated, there remains no basis for investigation. Because it is without a basis, it does not arise; and that is called Nirvāṇa.
When neither existence nor non-existence stands before the mind,"

Furthermore, it is stated in the *Rājaratnāvalī*: "Since there is no other possible resort, [the mind] becomes tranquil when it is without an object; for all the phenomena of the world are considered to be the fuel for the fire of consciousness, and having been burned by the flames of correct analytical investigation, that fire is extinguished."
To the question "How is both investigated?",
he says "existence," and so forth;
because existence and non-existence possess a mutual identity, there is no contradiction [between them].
He says that there is a distinction, namely,
"empty of both existence and non-existence";
for the natures of existence and non-existence are empty because the mind is devoid of a nature— whether singular or multiple— and is thus without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
For it is thus: that [cognition] is not one;

for if it were one, there would be no cognition appearing as variegated through the forms of blue and yellow, because it would follow that everything would be perceived as being included within the yellow or the blue.
Furthermore, there would be no cognition of even a blue [object] as having distinctions of front, back, and middle, nor as appearing gross;
for according to the principle that "that which possesses a distinction of spatial parts cannot be unitary," the manifestation would have to be merely a single atom.

Nor is it manifold; for if cognition were manifold, since the mind would be divided into atoms and there would be no perception of anything other than itself, each atom would be cognized by its own self-awareness, leading to the undesirable consequence that it would appear as a distinct manifestation for every single atom. A dual nature is not tenable, because such a mode of perception does not exist.
For in all cases, our perception is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);

yet we do not perceive through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) a consciousness of a nature that is both inclusive and exclusive, whether simultaneously or separately, nor do we perceive it through inference (*anumāna*), because the latter is preceded by the former.
And since we do not perceive [any such thing], how can we imagine that it possesses a nature consisting of both the inclusive (anugata) and the exclusive (vyāvṛtta)?
Now, there is this argument: consciousness, being variegated, has a gross form and is of the nature of self-awareness;

and this would not be possible without a nature consisting of both the inclusive and the exclusive. Therefore, that [nature] is imagined on the grounds that its existence would otherwise be inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*).

Therefore, that [reality] does not exist as anything other than the non-dual nature of the absence of conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*), because this is established most clearly through reasoning and the exhaustion of scriptural authority;
for this very reason, even arising is not tenable,
since there is a lack of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a causal relationship.
For the determination of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) occurs only when means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) function in a sequence of priority and posteriority.

It has been established that non-dual cognition—which is devoid of the two forms [of subject and object]—does not possess such sequential operation; nor is there any other cognition [to establish it], due to the absence of a means of valid cognition.

And since, in this way, there is no production at all because there is no means of valid cognition for a causal relationship, how then could there be [production] from self, from another, from both, or without a cause?
Thus, because there is no arising, even the state of being an entity does not exist for the mind;
for "being" (bhāva) is established only as a manifestation preceded by non-existence (asattā).
For this very reason, it also lacks the nature of non-existence consisting in its own cessation.
And because of the non-existence of the intrinsic nature of both existence and non-existence,
there is the non-existence of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*),
since those two are pervaded by [the reality] which is the substratum of existence and non-existence.
And since the pervaded is absent when the pervader is absent,
it follows that through this analysis, the state of being free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*)— that is, the state of emptiness— is understood;
and this indeed is the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*).
When one investigates with the eye of wisdom, and the light of right knowledge is present, there is the non-perception of all phenomena;
as it is said in the *Bhagavatī*:
"What is the wisdom-eye of the Blessed Buddhas, by which they do not see anything?"
Likewise, what is the vision of ultimate reality (*paramārthadarśana*)? It is the non-vision of all phenomena (*sarvadharmāṇām adarśanam*).
Therefore, even for those practitioners of reality (*tattvayogin*), while they are established in all modes of conduct and see all phenomena and non-phenomena, they do not [ultimately] see them;
it is precisely such a non-vision that is intended.

But it is not as if [the mind were absent] like that of one who is asleep or whose eyes are closed; for by the mere absence of mental attention (*amanasikāra*), since the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) have not been abandoned, the yogi would remain unliberated—just like one who has emerged from the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) and so forth—because passion and the other afflictions, rooted in the attachment to form and so forth, would arise once again.
Furthermore, the attachment to form and so forth, which is beginningless, is not abandoned merely by the avoidance of mental attention.
Otherwise, it would follow that even those who have attained the meditative absorption of non-perception (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*) and so forth have abandoned [the defilements];
furthermore, it is impossible to avoid attending to such objects as form without abandoning doubt regarding them,
just as one cannot avoid being burned without avoiding the fire.
Therefore, the certainty is this: because the seed of doubt has been removed, the attachment to form and so forth should be led away [and discarded], but not by being uprooted like a thorn.
Thus, by setting aside mental engagement with existence, non-existence, intrinsic nature, extrinsic nature, and so on, one should withdraw the mind from everything and not think of anything at all.

For the yogi who does not think in this way and who has previously served his guru for a long time, that very Blessed Lady Prajñā arises through the grace of the guru, having been attained [by him] beforehand.

Having directly realized, through the yoga of non-perception, that state which is beyond conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañcatā*)—whose nature is self-luminous because the distinctions between means of knowledge, objects of knowledge, and their results have ceased—and which is of the nature of supreme bliss due to the departure from the flood of suffering inherent in the cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) consisting of proliferation; and having reflected, "Oh, how great is the power of delusion (*moha*), by which these beings do not realize themselves as being of the very nature of *nirvāṇa*, and how indeed might I awaken them?", there arises a Great Compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) whose nature is non-objectification, taking as its object the entire world which is of that same [compassionate] nature.

Then one should perceive oneself as having arisen in the form of the maṇḍala, which is of that very nature—the self-nature of all phenomena, consisting of great compassion, and of non-dual nature with the Blessed Lady Prajñā, who is otherwise named Mahāmudrā, because they are of one essence.
At that time, the identity of emptiness and compassion is the non-conceptual yoga; that indeed is it.
"Withdrawal, as well as meditation, breath control, concentration, recollection, and meditative absorption—this is held to be the six-limbed yoga.
Thus is described the six-limbed yoga as stated in the *Samājottara*.
For instance, withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) is the grasping of objects by the senses as having the single flavor of emptiness, like a young girl beholding her own reflection in a mirror.
Then there is *dhyāna* (meditative concentration),

which consists of *vitarka* (initial inquiry) regarding reality, *vicāra* (sustained investigation) which is the examination of the nature of phenomena as being empty (*śūnyatā*), and the mental joy (*saumanasya*) that arises for one who thus investigates while facing toward entry into reality; from that comes great bliss (*mahāsukha*), such as the pliancy of the body (*kāyaprasrabdhi*).
Having practiced in this way, one-pointedness of mind consisting of wisdom, which is solely intent upon the emptiness of all phenomena, is the fifth [limb].

Then, the activity of the vital wind (*prāṇavāyu*), characterized by entry, abiding, and emergence through the path of the *avadhūtī* alone—once the *lalanā* and *rasanā* have been restrained—is breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

This is the thirteenth chapter. Then, the non-emergence from the *avadhūtī* and the settling of the vital wind, the vehicle of the mind, into the drop of bodhicitta, which is of a single flavor with emptiness, is retention (*dhāraṇā*).
And at that time, the *caṇḍālī* blazes by its very nature, and the moon, ignited by her, flows forth even more intensely.
Then, the immutable *bodhicitta* within the *vajramaṇi*, gradually becoming filled with the bliss of the *niṣyanda* and so forth, reaches a state of complete purity.

Thereafter, when the mind has entered into *dhāraṇā*, preceded by the appearance of signs, there arises the vision of the deities of the maṇḍala in the form of a reflection, free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpaka*). From that follows the radiation of manifold rays of light, and then the radiation throughout the three realms; this is *anusmṛti*.
Therefore, that very non-conceptual state is the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) whose nature is the Great Vajradhara—the body of gnosis consisting of the union of bliss and the syllable of yoga.

And thus, when the yogin is of the nature of the yoga of non-proliferated wisdom and means, he is then established by the Lords as being composed of all merit, composed of all gnosis, identical with the deities of the entire maṇḍala, and the embodiment of the entire system of the perfections (*pāramitā*).
As it has been said:
This is that supreme yoga, free from all conceptual constructions,
wherein established, the yogi becomes directly the omniscient Blessed One;
this is that supreme reality, consisting of wisdom and means, and auspicious.
"This very non-dual gnosis is the supreme bodhicitta," so it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna:
"That person who would cultivate bodhicitta for even a single moment..."
"It is impossible to calculate how great this mass of merit of his is;

it is said that the jewel of the supreme mind consists of nothing more than the removal of the gem of affliction—it is unassailable and cannot be carried off by the thieves of the afflictions and Māras.
With all this in mind, he says: "These are the purities of the mind."

For this very reason, these [perfections] take the form of great bliss (*mahāsukha*); because they are established right here on the level of the Vajra-holder, this constitutes the distinction of this [path] from the *pāramitānaya*.
But surely that [level] is itself the nature of non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*); so what is its distinction?
There is indeed a distinction, which consists precisely in the demonstration of suchness.

For instance, in the *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the great king of tantras, the *Śrī Buddhakapāla*, it is proclaimed that there is a great distinction because the powers (*bala*), the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*), and so forth— which in reality have the single flavor of emptiness— are not demonstrated as emptiness in the Śrāvaka system, whereas they are demonstrated as such in the Pāramitā system.

But surely, even for one who has attained the first dhyāna, happiness is taught—just as it is for a universal monarch (*cakravartin*)—so how much more so upon the penetration of both forms of selflessness?
For indeed, the first stage (*bhūmi*) is called "The Joyful" (*pramuditā*) precisely because of the abundance of exultation;
yet this is not innate bliss (*sahaja-sukha*).
For this very reason, there is neither great bliss nor that produced by skillful means in the stage of a beginner;
for even a needle’s eye does not experience equality with space merely by being called a "hole."
But was it not stated in the *Prajñāpāramitā* that there is the bliss of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?
This has indeed been stated,
but its means (*upāya*) has not been shown.
Because the innate great bliss that serves as the means has not been taught,
therefore that too must be understood through this very sequence;
why then would there be no enlightenment in the system of the Perfections?
Without the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), how could there even be the scent of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment?

Furthermore, even at the very limit of the fourfold [analysis], it is said that this necessarily depends upon this means (upāya). Enough with such detail; those who have understood the instructions will clearly perceive this distinction for themselves.

In order to demonstrate that touch— the primary object of the sense faculty and its corresponding cognition— is the means for achieving great bliss (*mahāsukha*), and that it takes the form of compassion and so forth as well as the five types of wisdom (*prajñā*), he says "therefore" and so on:
"I shall explain that which arises from the purification of the external wisdom, the body, and the object, as well as through the union with them, and of the internal body and cognition."
"Endowed with vision" means that seeing a beautiful woman is compassion (*karuṇā*), which is the separation from suffering;

embracing her is loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which is the union with happiness; the friction of the two organs is sympathetic joy (*muditā*), which is the non-separation from bliss; and through the cause of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), equanimity (*upekṣā*) is the absence of all conceptual constructions.
Thus, for one who is endowed with such cultivation and yoga regarding the knowledge of the internal body in the form of compassion and so forth— meaning,
one joined with the Mahāmudrā in the form of compassion and so forth— is not bound by passion and the like.
But [the Buddha] said that without the yoga of Mahāmudrā, the world is afflicted,
beginning with the words "from seeing" and so forth;
that fruit is somewhat greater than that.

Because everything has been concluded in this way, the result of joy and dejection—the arising of the threefold world—is stated to be empty; the implication is that even compassion and the other [virtues] are not causes for liberation without emptiness. Thus he concludes.
The triad beginning with "completely purified" refers to the object, the sense faculty, and consciousness.
Thus, for one devoted to such practice, he describes the transformation of food as it is encountered: "If," and so forth.
One should conceptualize the nectar as consisting of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta), such as feces, urine, and so forth, and as being composed of lamps;
not only that, but one's sexual play and the like, as well as the Mahāmudrā, should be viewed as having the form of the Mahāmudrā.
One who is endowed with such meditation attains accomplishment.
To the question "How? he says:
"The five" refers to the yoginīs such as the sister and so forth.

"Lakṣmī, the bestower of the Mahāmudrā" means that Lakṣmī, characterized by the perfection of one's own and others' welfare, is indeed the Mahāmudrā; when worshipped, she bestows that very [Mahāmudrā].
Therefore, he says "one should worship.
To the question "How? he replies: "By means of desire" (kāmatas).
Now, is it not the case that for these [goddesses], the supreme worship is indeed desire, and is that not a fault?
There is no fault, because he is not smeared.
Is it not true that desire itself is the smearing? No; for what is called "smearing" is the association of that yogin with envy and other such passions.
He is not afflicted by vices such as envy because of them;
but how can such worship lead to spiritual welfare, given that it involves a particular form of superimposition?
For superimposition (samāropa) is of two kinds: that which consists of reality (tattvarūpa) and that which does not consist of reality (atattvarūpa).

Among these, there is no fault in the superimposition of the self as consisting of reality, because—just like the superimposition of [the self] as a mother and so forth—it serves as a means to awakening (bodhi) through a traditional succession.
But would there not be a contradiction, since even the experience of some [of this] has been prohibited?

No; for action is of two kinds, distinguished as that which is originated (*samutthāpya*) and that which originates (*samutthāpaka*); therein, all bodily and vocal action is that which is originated, whereas mental action is that which originates.
And that is of two kinds:
consisting of non-greed and so forth, and its opposite;
therein, all bodily and vocal action arising from greed and so forth is unwholesome.
And that [which is motivated by greed] is prohibited;
however, everything arising from non-greed and so forth is indeed wholesome.
Furthermore, the yogi joined with the yoga of the non-dual Mahāmudrā perceives the entire world as consisting of non-greed and the other [wholesome roots].
Then, although he is engaged in all modes of conduct, because he is of the nature of the non-apprehension of the unwholesome, he is essentially wholesome; thus it says, "That yogi," and so forth,
meaning that reality is the intrinsic nature of Mahāmudrā.
Therefore, one is not stained by the defects of saṃsāra;
for this reason, the cultivation of the non-dual bodhicitta, whose nature is wisdom and skillful means, alone is the purifier of all sins and the bringer of all excellence.
As it was said by the venerable Ārya Nāgārjuna: "This Mahāyāna is supreme; this bodhicitta is the highest."
With focused minds, generate the spirit of enlightenment with diligence;
for there is no other means in cyclic existence for the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others that has ever been seen by the Buddhas prior to the spirit of enlightenment.
And it should be understood in this way:
this is that supreme yoga; therefore, it is worshipped by the Tathāgatas, and from it the arising of infinite yogas is proclaimed.
From that very source arises the emergence of infinite meditative absorptions (samādhi), as well as the mudrās, maṇḍalas, and mantras; from that, too, comes the twofold purity of yoga.

This concludes the commentary on the *Śrībuddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja*, titled *Abhayapaddhati*, concerning the rites of pacification (*śāntika*), enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), and whatever other [rites] arise from mantra.
As numerous as the grains of sand in the Ganges are the minor siddhis,
and as many other mudrā-siddhis as are renowned throughout the earth—
all these have been taught by Cittavajra as arising from this yoga.
And that which consists of the four stages conducive to penetration, the ten stages,
and the state of fruition— all that has arisen from this yoga. These are the sons of the Conquerors who have been, who will be, and who are now existing.
The great beings such as Lokeśa and others are also established right here;
for from this [source] arise all the Buddhas of the past, future, and present,
as well as those considered to be the Pratyekabuddhas and the assembly of Śrāvakas.

From the distinctions of yoga, conduct, and ritual action, up to the manifestation of the syllables (nirvāṇa), all these have emerged from this very yoga. As many as there are conceptualized forms arising through the power of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
so many are dependent upon that [yoga], for they lack stable strength.
Thus,

as long as the sprout of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) is not nourished by the flavors of sense objects, the wish-fulfilling tree of the Buddha-body (*buddhakāya-kalpataru*) does not manifest.

This has been stated by Saraha-pāda: "The sprout of the unsurpassed mind, if it is not watered by the pure juices of the sense-objects, how can it attain the state of a wish-fulfilling tree that pervades the sky and bestows fruit? (Thirteenth Chapter)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the *Śrī Buddhakapāla-mahātantra* composed by the scholar Abhayakaragupta.

Chapter Fourteen: The Recitation of Mantras, known as the Entreaty to the Mother Prajñā, which constitutes the fundamental cause of all tantras. "Then," and so forth: because she sports in great bliss (*mahāsukha*), the Goddess is the Mother, the embodiment of the Path.
Lakṣmī, whose nature is the fruit consisting of the perfection of attainment and abandonment,
is "terrible" because she is a source of terror for those without the spiritual lineage (agotra), yet she is "of great renown" and possesses celebrated fame.
Because she consists of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), she is affectionate;

because she possesses infinite miraculous transformations such as the mandala circle, and because she is non-different from great compassion (*mahākṛpā*) and great wisdom (*mahāprajñā*), the Goddess is the Great Seal (*mahāmudrā*), the perfection of her own welfare.

"He who teaches the fruit of great significance"—great significance is the state of Vajradhara; that itself is the supreme fruit of practicing the path. Because he teaches this to those to be trained, they praise him through the perfection of the welfare of others, praising him specifically by way of his teaching.
"Buddhas" and so forth refers to Vairocana and the other Buddhas;
"of whom" refers to that accomplishment which is beyond the scope of the Bodhisattvas;
and "goddess" refers to the Goddess.
"By a single sound" means that she is not one who first speaks what is difficult to understand and then reveals it through other words; rather,
she is a "great vessel," a vessel for all the great mundane and supramundane accomplishments (*siddhi*),
and she is the nature of the twenty-four yoginīs.

Regarding that accomplishment which Citrasenā spoke of as "this," namely the qualities of a Buddha such as the powers (*bala*) and the fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), may they also forgive me; for the meaning consisting of the cause and fruit of those qualities— which was concealed by the Supreme Victors from those to be trained and is extremely difficult to find— has been revealed by me in this tantra whose scope is so well-guarded.
The meaning is that since everything has been revealed by the supreme Victors, this teaching was delivered by them directly; therefore,
he says that one should not harbor resentment toward me for the imputation of the fault of teaching erroneously.
Regarding the phrase "May the excellent Victors be patient," there is a change in grammatical case (*vibhaktivipariṇāma*).

Having thus spoken the general rule for all systems, he states the procedure for initiation at the end with the words "Now," etc., in order to demonstrate that only those who have been initiated have the authority (*adhikāra*) here.
These are studied for the sake of the secret, wisdom, and knowledge empowerments; thus she is called the Great Goddess, the Mahādevī.
In the reading "chinneti tvayā channeti," the word "tasya" (of him) refers even to that which is pervasive.
Why is there such an effort to satisfy her with wisdom? To this he says:
she is worshipped by all the Buddhas;
for the tradition holds that the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā occurs precisely through the yoga of the Karmamudrā during the stages of cause and fruit.
To the question "How is it so?", he says:
"Brahmā and the others abide in this very wisdom; for they have the nature of great bliss, and wisdom is their support."
The fourteenth chapter of that [work] states that one should receive the initiation of the wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñānābhiṣeka*) according to the prescribed rule;
for this very reason, it explains the essential nature of the wisdom-knowledge,
beginning with the word "Indra" and so forth.
The sense faculty, as well as the object and so forth,
are characterized [as such] because of the statement: "The self is conceived as the mind, and the mind is the self."
Alternatively, the five aggregates of clinging, which are the objects of the designation "self," are the self;
all this is without intrinsic nature, and that wherein nothing is perceived is supreme bliss.

Supreme bliss (*paramānanda*) here is indeed innate bliss (*sahajānanda*); it is wisdom (*prajñā*), which has "knowledge" (*jñāna*) as another name, because of the disappearance of the superimposition of the senses and so forth.
As it is said in the *Dvikalpa Tantra*: "When supreme bliss, devoid of manifoldness, is attained in that moment..."
Thus, its attainment should be understood according to the sequence of arising,
and that has been explained in the first chapter.
He pays homage to supreme bliss itself as the cause, with the words "in that" and so forth; by whose arising— that is, by the arising of which innate bliss (sahajānanda)— [it occurs].

That which bows through the state of fruition by means of practice, following the sequence of attaining the stages conducive to penetration (*nirvedhabhāgīya*) and so forth; which is exultant and enriched on all sides with the peerless jewels of qualities such as the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), the powers (*bala*), and the grounds of self-confidence (*vaiśāradya*); which is beautiful due to the removal of the stains of all afflictions (*kleśa*) and is "Samantabhadra" (All-Good) because of its supreme joy; which dwells as the embodiment—the fourth body (*kāya*)—Vajradhara, within the hearts of the wise, the perfectly awakened Buddhas, in identity with them; and which, being free from all conceptual proliferation and distraction, is tranquil and beyond the sphere of speech and intellect.
For this very reason, having realized this [Self], Citrasena and the others will remain established in silence;
he will say: "Salutation to Him who is one, non-dual, supreme bliss, and who is awake due to being free from the sleep of all residual veils and latent impressions."
Thus, by this verse, that very wisdom-knowledge (*prajñājñāna*), having arisen in a specific form like water in the form of waves, is called the fourth consecration.
Furthermore, this Vajradhara, consisting of great bliss, is the source of all tantras.
This concludes the fourteenth chapter in the *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the *Śrībuddhakapāla-mahātantra* composed by the scholar Abhayākaragupta.

|| 14 || Having severed the delusion of cyclic existence and liberation through the lofty, auspicious, and radiant exposition of the path of the glorious heroic Heruka—the commentary on the *Śrī-Buddhakapāla-mahātantrarāja* titled *Abhayapaddhati*—may the world rest within that mandala; may I, however, for a long time assume the infinite forms of this Sage, bestowing vast and intense bliss upon every living being and forever destroying the web of conceptual proliferation. Thus speaks the master Abhaya of Vikramaśīla, whose words touch the very core of reality.
In the twenty-fifth year of the reign of Rāmapāla, he composed this [work].

By the request of Śrī Yakṣapāla—the son of the Lord of Magadha, who has conquered the non-dual Dharma for the benefit of the world, whose form is never diminished in its protection of the earth and the Fortune of Victory over the three worlds—this book was written for the fulfillment of his steadfast resolve. May it endure as the ground of rest for the exuberance of the supreme non-dual nectar arising from the root of bliss, a flight of stairs consisting of dense multitudes of sages and the playful presence of the Vajra-Maiden.

May this [work], which dwells within the creeper of the intentions of seekers who have accomplished their purpose through the glory of wisdom, bring satisfaction to us by filling us with the incomparable nectar of virtue.
Thus ends the *Abhayapaddhati*, a commentary on the *Śrī Buddhakapāla-mahātantra*,
the work of the venerable scholar-monk Abhayākaragupta.
This valid cognition, condensed into one hundred and sixteen verses, is like the true reality itself; let it be cherished in the hearts of the wise for their own adornment. Thus [ends the work].

* The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come into existence and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Then the Venerable Ānanda, having risen from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, bowed down with his head at the feet of the Blessed One, and said: “It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well has this been stated by the Blessed One: ‘Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come into existence and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. “Ānanda, it is because I have fully understood, as they really are, the gratification, the danger, and the escape regarding these four nutriments, that I have awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. “Blessed One, what is the gratification, what is the danger, and what is the escape regarding these four nutriments? “Ānanda, whatever pleasure and satisfaction arise in dependence on these four nutriments—this is the gratification. That these four nutriments are impermanent, suffering, subject to change, and characterized by the nature of decay—this is the danger. The complete dispassion toward these four nutriments, the relinquishing of them, the abandoning of them, the destruction of them, the renunciation of them, and the non-attachment to them—this is the escape. Having heard this, the Venerable Ānanda was delighted and rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words. He then rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, and keeping him on his right, departed. Then the Venerable Ānanda, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, soon realized through direct knowledge in this very life that unsurpassed liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, for the sake of which sons of noble family rightly go forth from the household life into homelessness. He knew: “Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what had to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being. And the Venerable Ānanda became one of the arahants.
